76  Scientific Writing

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

A research paper is the instrument through which a discovery becomes knowledge. A result that is not written down does not exist scientifically; a result written badly exists only for the handful of readers willing to excavate it. This chapter treats scientific writing not as cosmetic polish applied after the “real” work but as an integral part of the research itself—a design problem with its own constraints, its own failure modes, and its own measurable quality. The audience is the marketing scholar who has a finding and now faces the harder task of convincing a skeptical editor, two or three adversarial reviewers, and an indifferent field that the finding is correct, novel, and important.

The economics of the situation are unforgiving. The top journals in marketing—the Journal of Marketing (JM), the Journal of Marketing Research (JMR), Marketing Science, and the Journal of Consumer Research (JCR), collectively the “top-4”—desk-reject a large share of submissions and ultimately accept only a small fraction of what is sent to them. A reviewer reads dozens of papers a year as unpaid labor and forms a judgment within the first few pages. The paper that survives is not merely the one with the best result; it is the one whose argument the reviewer can reconstruct without effort and whose contribution the reviewer can state in a sentence. Writing is therefore a competitive technology, and this chapter develops it as one.

The chapter proceeds from architecture to sentence. We begin with the structure of a paper—the canonical section sequence and what each section is for—and formalize the underlying logical scaffold. We then treat the hardest and most consequential task, framing the contribution, and then the two genres the hypo-deductive template serves badly—the descriptive paper, which contributes a pattern, and the abductive paper, which reasons from a pattern to the best available explanation. Next comes the part of the paper where framing lives or dies: the front end (title, abstract, introduction). We turn next to the specific demands of writing for the top-4, where the contribution bar is highest. We close with clarity and revision: the sentence-level craft that makes an argument legible, the measurement of readability, and the disciplined process of responding to reviewers. Throughout, the stance is the house stance— intuition first, then the formal structure that makes the intuition operational.

76.1 The Structure of a Paper

76.1.1 The canonical sections and their tenses

Empirical marketing papers share a near-universal skeleton, sometimes abbreviated IMRaD (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) with literature review and conclusions bracketing the core. Each section answers one question and only one, and—this is a point novices routinely miss—each section has a default verb tense that signals the epistemic status of its claims. Completed actions take the simple past (“we estimated”, “respondents rated”); established knowledge and the paper’s own ongoing argument take the present (“the effect is”, “Table 2 reports”); prior literature as a stream that continues into the present takes the present perfect (“researchers have shown”). Table 76.1 collects the sections, their purposes, approximate lengths, and tense conventions.

The discipline of one-question-per-section is what gives a paper its navigability. A reader who wants to know what you did turns to Methods and finds only that; a reader who wants to know why it matters turns to the Discussion and is not detained by procedure. Violations—results smuggled into the methods, mechanism speculation buried in the results—are the most common structural defect flagged in review, because they force the reader to hold the paper’s logic in their head rather than read it off the page.

A scientific paper is not a chronological record of what the researcher did. It is a reconstructed argument, organized so that the reader can verify the conclusion with minimum effort. The order of discovery and the order of exposition are different things, and conflating them is the surest route to an unreadable manuscript.

76.1.2 The argument as a logical object

Underneath the section skeleton sits a logical scaffold that the prose merely dresses. Make it explicit. A confirmatory empirical paper advances a chain

\[ \underbrace{P}_{\text{problem}} \;\Rightarrow\; \underbrace{G}_{\text{gap}} \;\Rightarrow\; \underbrace{H}_{\text{hypotheses}} \;\Rightarrow\; \underbrace{D}_{\text{design}} \;\Rightarrow\; \underbrace{R}_{\text{results}} \;\Rightarrow\; \underbrace{C}_{\text{contribution}} \tag{76.1}\]

in which every arrow is a claim the reader can refuse to grant. The problem \(P\) must be real (someone cares about the answer); the gap \(G\) must be genuine (the answer is not already known); the hypotheses \(H\) must follow from a theory and be falsifiable; the design \(D\) must be capable of discriminating \(H\) from its negation; the results \(R\) must actually bear on \(H\); and the contribution \(C\) must be what \(R\) licenses, not more. A paper fails at whichever arrow is weakest, and the writing task is to make each arrow as short and as forced as possible. Many rejections that are phrased as “not enough contribution” are in fact broken arrows: a gap that turns out to be already filled (\(G\)), or a design that cannot separate the focal hypothesis from a confound (\(D \not\Rightarrow R\)).

The conceptual or theory paper substitutes a different chain—a construct is defined, related to existing constructs, and shown to do explanatory work—but the demand for unbroken arrows is identical. Figure 76.1 renders the canonical flow and shows where each link in Equation 76.1 is forged.

The dashed promise–payoff loop in Figure 76.1 is the structural heart of a paper. The introduction makes a promise—“we will show that \(X\) causes \(Y\) through mechanism \(M\)”—and the discussion must redeem exactly that promise, no more and no less. A paper that promises a causal claim and delivers a correlation, or that delivers a richer finding than it promised and never updates the framing, reads as incoherent even when every individual sentence is sound.

76.1.3 Paper types

The skeleton flexes with the paper’s type, and naming the type early orients both writer and reviewer. Four types recur. A research paper tests hypotheses and reports findings; its contribution lives in \(H \Rightarrow R\). A research paper can also build theory inductively instead of testing it, naming a new construct from qualitative evidence (Section 76.12). A methods paper proposes a new estimator, design, or measurement instrument; its contribution is that the method recovers something prior methods could not, so the burden is a demonstration—often on synthetic data with known ground truth—that it works and a comparison against incumbents. Its design-science variant, common in information systems, has its own architecture (Section 76.9). When the instrument is a new variable built from text or another unstructured source, the burden shifts from ground truth to validation against outcomes (Section 76.13). A review paper consolidates a domain, and its contribution is organization: a taxonomy, an integrative framework, or an agenda that practitioners and scholars did not previously have. A conceptual or discussion paper advances or critiques theory, trading empirical evidence for argumentative rigor. The reviewer evaluates each type against a different standard, and a paper that does not signal its type invites evaluation against the wrong one.

76.2 Framing the Contribution

76.2.1 What a contribution is

The single most important sentence in a paper is the one that states its contribution, and the most common reason good work is rejected is that this sentence is missing, vague, or overclaimed. Define the contribution formally. Let \(\mathcal{K}\) denote the field’s existing knowledge—the set of claims a competent reader already accepts before reading the paper. A paper’s contribution is the increment

\[ \Delta\mathcal{K} \;=\; \mathcal{K}_{\text{after}} \setminus \mathcal{K}_{\text{before}}, \tag{76.2}\]

the set of claims that a reader is licensed to accept after reading the paper and was not licensed to accept before. Three properties make \(\Delta\mathcal{K}\) publishable, and reviewers probe each one explicitly:

  • Novelty (\(\Delta\mathcal{K} \neq \varnothing\)): the increment is non-empty. If every claim in the paper already belonged to \(\mathcal{K}_{\text{before}}\), there is no contribution, however well executed the study.
  • Validity (\(\Delta\mathcal{K}\) is warranted): the increment is actually licensed by the evidence and argument. Overclaiming—asserting elements of \(\Delta\mathcal{K}\) that the design \(D\) cannot support—is the fastest route to a reviewer’s “the conclusions outrun the data”.
  • Importance (\(|\Delta\mathcal{K}|\) matters): the increment is one the field cares about. A true, novel, but trivial claim clears the first two bars and fails the third, and “importance” is precisely the bar that rises from a field journal to the top-4.

Two broad species of contribution recur in marketing, and a paper should know which it is making. A substantive contribution changes what we believe about a marketing phenomenon—that brand prominence signals status through quiet versus loud cues, say, or that responding to online reviews trades complaint quantity for depth (see Chapter 12). A methodological contribution changes how we can learn about phenomena—a new identification strategy, a scalable text measure, a more efficient estimator. The strongest papers often pair a methodological advance with the substantive finding it unlocks, but a paper that is fuzzy about which kind of increment it offers will be read as offering neither.

76.2.2 The contribution statement and the framing trap

A contribution should be expressible as a single declarative sentence of the form “We show that [claim], which prior work did not establish because [reason], using [design].” The clause “which prior work did not establish” is the gap \(G\) of Equation 76.1 made explicit, and it must be true: nothing destroys credibility faster than a literature-savvy reviewer who knows the claimed gap was filled years ago. Conversely, a contribution can be undersold. Authors who have lived inside a problem for years often state their finding in the narrow terms in which they discovered it, missing the more general claim the evidence actually supports. The discipline is to state the most general claim that \(R\) licenses and not one inch more.

Framing is the act of choosing which \(\mathcal{K}_{\text{before}}\) to write against— which conversation the paper joins—and it is a genuine strategic choice, not a neutral description. The same result can be framed as a contribution to several literatures, and the framing determines the reference set, the reviewers, and the perceived importance. A study of how customers respond to a salesperson’s language, for instance, could be framed against the persuasion literature, the frontline-service literature, or the computational-text-analysis literature, and the right choice depends on where the increment \(\Delta\mathcal{K}\) is largest and the audience most receptive. The framing trap is to choose the literature in which the result is most surprising rather than the one in which it is most defensible; surprise attracts an editor’s eye but invites reviewers who hold the strongest priors against the claim.

76.2.3 Setting Up a Question Whose Answer Is Not Already Known

The framing trap above has a constructive counterpart. A paper is read when its question is genuinely open—when a well-informed reader, having finished the introduction, could not confidently guess the result. Most manuscripts fail this test in the first two pages, and the usual reason is that they motivate with a gap rather than a question. “Prior work has not examined \(X\)” tells the reader that something is missing, invites the reply that it may be missing for good reason, and quietly promises that \(X\) will turn out to matter. Everyone knows how that paper ends.

The strongest available move is to assemble two established literatures that imply opposite answers, or that block the two obvious remedies, and then let the data adjudicate. Tanlamai, Khern-am-nuai, and Cohen (2026) is a compact instance, and it is worth reading as a piece of construction rather than for its result (Section 69.10.3.1).

The setup takes two moves. First, decades of evidence establish that houses in white-dominant neighborhoods sell above otherwise-similar houses in minority-dominant neighborhoods, and the literature attributes the gap to human bias. The implied remedy—take the human out of the loop—is the reader’s own next thought, which is exactly why the second move lands: recent work shows the gap is not fixed by conventional AI models, including those designed specifically to address discrimination. Machine bias closes the escape route that human bias opened.

With both remedies blocked, “what does a generative model do here?” becomes a question a reader cannot answer from the armchair. A case runs each way. Generative models are trained on human-produced text and should inherit human bias; they are also statistical predictors and should inherit the proxy encoding that defeats conventional models. Yet they represent a property differently than a hedonic regression over neighborhood features does, and it is not obvious that the same proxies survive that representation. The paper reports that generative AI narrows the gap—and the finding is interesting only because the framing made both directions live beforehand.

Three rules generalize from this.

Both branches must be publishable before you know which one you have. Write the question so that each answer is a contribution, ideally as an explicit pair: if the gap narrows, then \(X\); if it widens, then \(Y\). If only one branch is a paper, the introduction is doing advocacy, and reviewers detect this even when they cannot name it. This is also the honest form of the framing: it is what you would have pre-registered.

A counter-intuitive result raises the evidentiary bar rather than lowering it. Surprise is not a contribution by itself; it is a debt. The reader’s first hypothesis is that something is wrong with the measurement, so a paper of this shape owes a mechanism section, and owes it as a real analysis rather than a paragraph of speculation (Section 44.9, Section 76.6). Papers that lead with a surprising headline and defer the mechanism to “future research” are the ones that fail to replicate.

The two literatures must be summarized in terms their own authors would accept. The move degrades into a straw man the moment either position is flattened to make the opposition sharper. The workable test: write your one-sentence characterization of each literature, and ask whether a proponent would sign it. If either would object, the tension you have constructed is between caricatures, and a referee drawn from that literature will be the one to say so.

76.3 The Descriptive Paper

The template assumed so far—theory, hypotheses, identification, test—is not the only publishable shape, and treating it as such quietly rules out a class of papers the field needs. A descriptive paper establishes what a phenomenon looks like without claiming to have identified a causal effect within it. Its increment \(\Delta\mathcal{K}\) consists of pattern claims: this outcome co-occurs with that antecedent, this population sorts into these categories, this quantity has moved this way over this period.

The genre has explicit methodological warrant. Helfat (2007) argues that stylized facts are a legitimate and necessary input to theory development, because a theory can only be built against a phenomenon whose shape is known. Hambrick (2007) goes further, arguing that the field’s insistence on a theoretical contribution in every paper suppresses precisely the descriptive work theory needs to feed on. Neither position licenses atheoretical data-dumping: Sutton and Staw (1995) is equally clear that data, variables, and diagrams are not themselves theory. The reconciliation is that a descriptive paper contributes a pattern, states it as a pattern, and lets the theoretical payoff be the discipline the pattern imposes on subsequent explanation.

Choudhury, Moeen, and Wormald (2026) supply the positive account. Abduction—the mode of inference that formulates candidate explanations for an unexplained phenomenon—is a distinct research design rather than a deduction that failed to find support. Their treatment distinguishes the abductive trigger (the anomalous observation that starts the inquiry) from creative abduction (generating candidate explanations) and selective abduction (winnowing them), and is explicit that abduction admits no fixed template. That absence of a template is exactly why descriptive papers need to make their design visible on the page: a reader cannot infer it from convention.

76.3.1 What makes a descriptive contribution defensible

Five design choices separate a descriptive paper that publishes from one that reads as a set of cross-tabulations. Table 76.2 states them alongside a worked example: Moeen (2026), which maps founder knowledge origin onto mode of economic value capture in U.S. medical device start-ups and is developed substantively in Chapter 30.

The fifth row deserves emphasis because it is the one most often omitted. A descriptive paper that reports only the clean correspondence has documented a stereotype: academics do this, employees do that. The reader has no way to tell whether the operative variable is the credential or the knowledge. Reporting the cases that break the correspondence, and showing that they break it in the direction the proposed mechanism predicts, converts the pattern into an explanation candidate. This is selective abduction performed in public.

76.3.2 How the contribution sentence changes

The contribution sentence of Section 76.2 still applies, with the causal verb removed and the boundary stated. Rather than “we show that \(X\) causes \(Y\),” a descriptive paper claims “we establish that \(X\) and \(Y\) correspond in population \(P\), which prior work had not documented because it lacked [data/classification/setting], and we show the correspondence tracks \(M\) rather than \(X\) itself.” The final clause is what makes the paper theory-relevant without overclaiming, and it should be paired with an explicit statement of what the design cannot support. Reviewers punish descriptive papers that reach; they reward the ones that name their own ceiling. Stating “we do not claim founder origin is exogenous” in the paper is strictly better than having a reviewer state it for you.

76.3.3 Norms differ by field, and the difference is not subtle

This genre travels much better in Organization Science, Strategic Management Journal, and Strategy Science than in JM, JMR, or Marketing Science, where the descriptive lane is narrower and more codified. In marketing it runs mainly through three channels: empirical generalizations, in which a regularity is established across many datasets and contexts; new-data-source papers, in which the contribution is a measurement capability and the first look it affords; and stylized-facts sections embedded inside otherwise structural or causal papers, where description motivates the model rather than standing alone. Bart J. Bronnenberg, Dhar, and Dubé (2009) is the canonical marketing-side exemplar of the standalone form—a persistent geographic pattern in brand shares, a scaffold for interpreting it, and no causal overclaim.

On the management side, SMJ publishes papers that name the genre in the abstract. C. Liu and Shi (2026) describe their study as taking a “question-driven approach”: does liberal institutional ownership show up in a firm’s symbolic climate actions, its substantive ones, or neither? The answer is reported as associations, not effects, and several rows of Table 76.2 are visible in it. The antecedent comes from an external paper trail (the investors’ political donations), not from the authors’ judgment. The cuts that carry the finding (consistent donors, dedicated investors, firms without CEO duality) do the off-diagonal work of showing where the pattern holds and where it fails. The finding also turns on a dated split, 2016 onward, which the authors tie to rising political polarization. Whether that break was fixed before the estimation is exactly what the third row asks a reader to check, because a break chosen after looking at the data is a forking path. The substance is developed in Section 26.7.

Management Science publishes the genre as well, through its organizations department. De Stefano and Bidwell (2026) relate the breadth of an employee’s project portfolio to promotion inside one services firm, and their limitations section says in so many words that the results are correlational. Two specification choices do the work that identification would do elsewhere. First, the regressor is split by timing. Breadth in the current year and breadth accumulated before it enter separately, because the first is contaminated by selection (poorly matched employees keep switching projects) and the second much less so. The two coefficients take opposite signs, which a single cumulative measure would have blended. Second, the main models leave out the performance rating, on the argument that breadth plausibly works through performance and a mediator is a bad control. The rating is then added in a separate column so the reader can see how much the estimates move. Neither choice makes the estimates causal. Each tells the reader which rival account a coefficient has been protected against, and that is the most a descriptive design can offer. The substance is in Section 30.4.

The practical implication is a targeting decision made before writing. A descriptive paper aimed at a marketing journal usually needs one of the three channels above as its declared home; the same paper aimed at a management journal can stand on the stylized-facts warrant directly. Authors who write the management version and submit it to the marketing journal receive a predictable review: interesting, but what is the identification?

76.3.4 From a New Measure to a Model: When the Facts Cannot Choose

Of the three marketing channels, the new-data-source paper is the one most students will write first: the contribution is a measurement capability and the first look it affords. Its characteristic weakness is the one a referee names in the opening paragraph of the report. The facts are new, but what do they mean? Often the facts are consistent with two mechanisms that carry opposite implications, and no amount of further description will separate them. The paper then has two honest options. It can find a design that identifies the mechanism, or it can write down a model in which the mechanisms make different predictions and let the measured facts discipline it. The second route is how a measurement paper reaches a top general-interest journal when no experiment is available, and Lee (2026) is a compact specimen.

Lee measures something that had been measured mainly for large, established firms (Guiso, Sapienza, and Zingales 2015; Li et al. 2021): the corporate culture that start-ups advertise to job seekers, read from their postings on an online job board. Table 76.3 traces how the paper moves from that measure to a question the facts cannot answer, and then to a model that answers it.

(Only the published abstract was accessible when this section was written. The article is not open access, and the working-paper copy sits behind a bot check. The table records the paper’s moves as its abstract states them, and the model below is a stylized illustration written for this chapter, not Lee’s.)

It is worth seeing concretely why the null forces a model. A zero outcome gap between adopters and non-adopters is evidence of a zero effect only if adoption is unrelated to the firm’s underlying quality. If cash-poor firms value a 5% wage saving more, as they should, adopters are negatively selected, and a genuine productivity effect can be offset exactly by that selection. The chunk below builds two worlds. In World A the culture is purely a cost device: it has no productivity effect, and adoption is unrelated to firm quality. In World B the culture raises outcomes by 0.25 standard deviations, but the value of the wage saving falls with productivity, so weaker firms adopt more. Both worlds are tuned to the same adoption rate and the same outcome gap.

Code
# A stylized adoption model written for this illustration; it is not Lee's model.
# theta is a firm's latent productivity, which the researcher never sees; f is a
# noisy observable proxy for it (funding raised, say). Advertising the
# worker-centered culture (W = 1) is worth
#   s0 * exp(-rho * theta)   the labor-cost saving, worth more to cash-poor firms
#   + delta                  any productivity gain, which also raises the outcome
#   - K + u                  a fixed cost of sustaining the claim, and a taste shock
# and the outcome is y = theta + delta * W + e. Workers' taste for the culture
# (the wage discount and the application premium) is the same in both worlds.
s0 <- 0.25; sig_u <- 0.5

draw_world <- function(delta, rho, K, n = 5000, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  theta <- rnorm(n); f <- theta + rnorm(n)
  W <- as.integer(s0 * exp(-rho * theta) + delta - K + rlogis(n, scale = sig_u) > 0)
  data.frame(f, W, y = theta + delta * W + rnorm(n))
}
facts <- function(d) c(
  `Adoption share`        = mean(d$W),
  `Outcome gap`           = mean(d$y[d$W == 1]) - mean(d$y[d$W == 0]),
  `Adoption slope on f`   = unname(coef(lm(W ~ f, data = d))[2]))

world_A <- draw_world(delta = 0,    rho = 0,     K = 0.475)  # cost device only
world_B <- draw_world(delta = 0.25, rho = 0.425, K = 0.747)  # productivity, masked
knitr::kable(rbind(`World A: cost saving only` = facts(world_A),
                   `World B: productivity effect, selected adoption` = facts(world_B)),
             digits = 3,
             caption = "Two worlds, one set of headline facts. The adoption slope is the moment the headline facts do not use.")
Two worlds, one set of headline facts. The adoption slope is the moment the headline facts do not use.
Adoption share Outcome gap Adoption slope on f
World A: cost saving only 0.383 -0.028 -0.002
World B: productivity effect, selected adoption 0.385 0.003 -0.027
Code

# Model-implied moments, computed from adoption probabilities on a large
# simulated panel of firms (the same draws for every parameter value).
set.seed(99); th_s <- rnorm(20000); f_s <- th_s + rnorm(20000)
implied <- function(delta, rho, K) {
  S <- s0 * exp(-rho * th_s)
  p <- plogis((S + delta - K) / sig_u)
  c(adopt = mean(p),
    gap   = sum(p * (th_s + delta)) / sum(p) - sum((1 - p) * th_s) / sum(1 - p),
    slope = cov(p, f_s) / var(f_s),
    cost_share = sum(p * (S > delta)) / sum(p))   # adopters whose cost motive is larger
}
# For a candidate delta, find the (rho, K) that reproduce the two headline facts.
fit_headline <- function(delta, obs) {
  K_for <- function(rho) uniroot(function(K)
    implied(delta, rho, K)[["adopt"]] - obs[["Adoption share"]], c(-5, 10))$root
  rho <- uniroot(function(r)
    implied(delta, r, K_for(r))[["gap"]] - obs[["Outcome gap"]], c(-3, 5))$root
  c(delta = delta, rho = rho, K = K_for(rho))
}

obs <- facts(world_B)
ridge <- t(sapply(c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4), function(dl) {
  par <- fit_headline(dl, obs)
  c(par[1:2], implied(par[1], par[2], par[3])[c("adopt", "gap", "slope", "cost_share")])
}))
colnames(ridge) <- c("Productivity effect", "Selection strength", "Adoption share",
                     "Outcome gap", "Adoption slope", "Cost-motivated share")
knitr::kable(ridge, digits = 3,
             caption = "Every candidate productivity effect fits the headline facts of World B exactly; only the implied adoption slope differs.")
Every candidate productivity effect fits the headline facts of World B exactly; only the implied adoption slope differs.
Productivity effect Selection strength Adoption share Outcome gap Adoption slope Cost-motivated share
0.0 -0.006 0.385 0.003 0.000 1.000
0.1 0.190 0.385 0.003 -0.011 1.000
0.2 0.368 0.385 0.003 -0.023 0.764
0.3 0.523 0.385 0.003 -0.035 0.441
0.4 0.664 0.385 0.003 -0.047 0.333
Code

# The third moment picks the point on the ridge.
d_hat <- uniroot(function(dl) {
  p <- fit_headline(dl, obs); implied(p[1], p[2], p[3])[["slope"]] - obs[["Adoption slope on f"]]
}, c(0, 0.45))$root
p_hat <- fit_headline(d_hat, obs)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  ` ` = c("True (World B)", "Recovered from three moments"),
  `Productivity effect` = c(0.25, d_hat),
  `Cost-motivated share of adopters` = c(implied(0.25, 0.425, 0.747)[["cost_share"]],
                                         implied(p_hat[1], p_hat[2], p_hat[3])[["cost_share"]]),
  check.names = FALSE), digits = 3,
  caption = "Adding the adoption slope identifies the productivity effect and the distribution of motives.")
Adding the adoption slope identifies the productivity effect and the distribution of motives.
Productivity effect Cost-motivated share of adopters
True (World B) 0.250 0.565
Recovered from three moments 0.234 0.622

The first table is the referee’s problem in miniature. Both worlds show the same adoption share (about 0.38) and an outcome gap that no sample of this size could tell from zero; its standard error is about 0.04. The wage discount and the application premium come from workers’ taste and are identical by construction. The second table shows why more description of the same facts cannot help. For every candidate productivity effect from 0 to 0.4 there is a selection strength that reproduces the headline facts exactly, so the facts trace a ridge, not a point. What breaks the tie is a prediction the model makes and the headline facts do not use. If selection is masking a productivity effect, adoption must fall with an observable proxy for firm quality, and the steeper the fall, the larger the effect it hides. In World B the slope is −0.027 with a standard error near 0.005, so it is easily detected. Matching that one extra moment picks a point on the ridge and recovers an effect of 0.23 against a true 0.25. It also returns a quantity no regression could report: the share of adopters for whom the cost saving, rather than the productivity gain, is the larger motive. The recovered share is 0.62 against a true 0.57.

Five lessons carry over to any measurement paper that is tempted to add a model.

  1. The facts ask for the model. Its question is the one the reduced form leaves open, and the paper says so before the model appears. A model appended to answer a question nobody raised reads as decoration.
  2. The measured facts discipline the model. The wage discount is not only a finding; it sets the size of the cost motive. A model whose parameters owe nothing to the paper’s own measurements throws away the contribution the paper has already made.
  3. Name the moment that identifies the mechanism. Say which feature of the data separates the hypotheses and why the headline facts could not. In the toy it is the adoption gradient; in a real paper it may be an entry margin, a distribution rather than a mean, or a response to a shock.
  4. Deliver a quantity, not a verdict. “Many firms adopt primarily for cost savings” is a statement about the distribution of motives across firms, which a model can return and a regression cannot.
  5. Keep the model as small as the question. The toy needs three parameters to settle one question. Every additional primitive is another link in Equation 76.1 that a referee may refuse to grant.

The paper’s history suggests that the third and fourth lessons were learned in revision. An earlier version circulated in 2022 as a Singapore Management University working paper. As indexed there, its abstract presented the model as showing that financially constrained start-ups have an incentive to advertise the culture workers prefer, even though without the constraint they would not. The published abstract instead poses the model as a contest between two named mechanisms, cost savings and productivity, and reports which one dominates. The model’s job shifted from rationalizing a fact to adjudicating between explanations of it, and that is the form in which the paper was published. (The working-paper abstract was read through a search index, not from the document itself.)

A descriptive paper that stops at the pattern is one genre; a paper that goes on to argue for a particular explanation of that pattern is another, and it needs a reporting structure of its own. That is the subject of Section 76.4.

76.4 The Abductive Paper and the PEEBI Structure

A descriptive paper stops at the pattern. A large class of empirical papers does not: it commits to an explanation of the pattern that was constructed after the pattern was seen, and that was never tested deductively because it did not exist before the data did. This is abduction, or inference to the best explanation (IBE), and it produces a great deal of what marketing knows. The difficulty is not the inference—it is the testimony. Pillai et al. (2026) observe that although scholars employ abduction routinely, there is no agreed-upon structure for reporting it, and the hypo-deductive reporting template does not align with the epistemology of abduction. They propose one, PEEBI, a five-section structure in which the authors take prior knowledge and theories, establish the context and observations worthy of interest, identify and evaluate candidate explanations for the observed patterns, determine the best explanation and their reasoning for accepting it, and abstract that explanation to a more generalizable theoretical contribution. The structure “advances knowledge in a modest, stepwise fashion” and is designed to foreground the author’s judgment rather than hide it.

76.4.1 Why the deductive template misreports abductive work

The template of Section 76.1 asks the reader to grant a chain that begins with a hypothesis and ends with a test. Abductive work runs the other way: the observation comes first, the candidate explanations are generated by the author rather than handed down by prior theory, and the evidence that discriminates among them is assembled afterward. Table 76.4 contrasts what each mode actually asks of a reader.

Forcing abductive work into the deductive template requires a small fiction: the explanation is presented as though it preceded the data. The field already has a name for the vicious version of that fiction—HARKing—and the reason abduction is not HARKing is disclosure: the order of discovery is stated, the rival explanations are named, and the residual uncertainty is quantified or at least bounded. The deductive template deletes precisely those three things. It does not merely misfit the work; it removes the information that licenses the conclusion.

76.4.2 The five acts

Table 76.5 states the five sections, what each one owes the reader, and where it goes in a manuscript aimed at a marketing journal, since few marketing editors will accept section headings named after an epistemology.

The move that does the work is the third act. In a conventional marketing paper, alternative explanations are a defensive appendix written to preempt reviewer objections; in an abductive paper they are the argument. A reader who is shown four candidates, the evidence for and against each, and the author’s reasoning for preferring one has been given the material to disagree—which is the point. Pillai et al. (2026) frame this as elevating the reader’s role: the paper’s job is to supply the information a reader needs to reach a judgment, not to foreclose it.

76.4.3 The abductive chain

The counterpart to Equation 76.1 runs

\[ \underbrace{O}_{\text{observation}} \;\Rightarrow\; \underbrace{\mathcal{E} = \{E_1, \dots, E_K\}}_{\text{candidate set}} \;\Rightarrow\; \underbrace{V}_{\text{evaluation}} \;\Rightarrow\; \underbrace{E^{*}}_{\text{best explanation}} \;\Rightarrow\; \underbrace{T}_{\text{abstraction}} \tag{76.3}\]

and, as before, every arrow is a claim the reader may refuse to grant. The observation \(O\) must be real and genuinely surprising against the priors—a pattern that everyone expected is not an abductive trigger. The candidate set \(\mathcal{E}\) must be adequate: it must contain the explanation a hostile expert would propose, which is the arrow that breaks most often. The evaluation \(V\) must apply the same standard to every candidate; searching hard for evidence that supports \(E_1\) and casually for evidence against it is the abductive analogue of a rigged specification search. The selection \(E^{*}\) must dominate the survivors on stated grounds rather than on the author’s enthusiasm. And the abstraction \(T\) must not outrun the case: one setting supports a mechanism claim, not a law.

Failure at each arrow has a diagnostic signature in reviews. A weak \(O\) draws “this is well known.” A thin \(\mathcal{E}\) draws “the authors have not ruled out…” An asymmetric \(V\) draws “the evidence for the preferred story is treated differently from the evidence against it.” An overreaching \(T\) draws “the contribution is not supported by a single context.”

76.4.4 What makes an explanation “best”

The word best carries the whole burden, and Pillai, Goldfarb, and Kirsch (2024) unpack it along two dimensions that do not coincide. An explanation is lovely when it is useful, general, and provides meaning; it is likely when it is close to the truth. Loveliness is what makes a mechanism worth having; likeliness is what makes it true. A managerially elegant story about why a promotion worked can be extremely lovely and quite unlikely, and a precisely estimated coefficient can be likely and entirely unlovely. Their argument is that interpreting observational results requires an understanding of context that statistical analysis alone cannot supply, and that historical methods—hermeneutics, contextualization, and source criticism—help scholars both generate new candidate explanations and judge and balance the virtues that make one explanation better than another.

In marketing the contextual sources are close at hand and systematically underused: category and brand histories, trade press, retailer and manufacturer archives, advertising archives, regulatory filings, and interviews with the people who made the decisions in the data. A researcher who knows that a category was restructured by a distribution change in 1998 has a candidate explanation that no amount of panel-data variance decomposition will hand them.

The practical artifact this yields is a candidate-explanation table, written early and revised as evidence accumulates. Table 76.6 sketches its form for a stylized marketing pattern—a brand’s share is persistently higher in markets it entered first—and it is the single most useful document a student can produce before writing an abductive paper, because it makes the completeness of \(\mathcal{E}\) visible to the author.

76.4.5 A worked example, reconstructed

Marketing has abductive exemplars; what it lacks is the habit of labeling them. Read as a two-paper arc, Bart J. Bronnenberg, Dhar, and Dubé (2009) and B. J. Bronnenberg, Dubé, and Gentzkow (2012) instantiate the chain in Equation 76.3 almost exactly—though neither paper presents itself in these terms, and the reconstruction is ours.

The first paper establishes: brand shares in consumer packaged goods differ persistently across U.S. geographic markets, and the differences track the brand’s early entry more than a century back. Against the priors of a field that models share as a function of current marketing mix, that is a genuine surprise, and the paper states it as a pattern rather than as an effect. The candidate set is the obvious one—something on the demand side (consumers in these markets simply prefer this brand, for reasons formed long ago) versus something on the supply side (the early entrant enjoys durable cost, distribution, or retail advantages there).

Market-level data cannot separate those candidates, and this is where an abductive paper either finds a discriminating observation or admits it cannot. The second paper finds one: consumers who move between markets carry their preferences with them, converging only slowly toward their new market’s shares. Movers separate the two candidates cleanly, because a consumer-side stock travels with the consumer while a supply-side advantage does not. That is act four performed in public—the best explanation determined, with the reasoning for accepting it visible—and the abstraction in act five is the one that made the work matter beyond CPG: brand preference behaves as an accumulated consumer-side capital stock with a very long half-life.

Two features of the arc are worth copying. The discriminating evidence was sought after the candidates were named, not before—the honest order, and the one PEEBI asks you to report. And the abstraction stops where the evidence stops: a claim about how preferences persist and transfer, not a claim that early entry causes share everywhere.

76.4.6 Getting an abductive paper through a marketing review

The genre travels less easily in JM, JMR, and Marketing Science than in SMJ or Organization Science, for the reason given in Section 76.3: the default reviewer question in marketing is “what is the identification?” Three adjustments carry most of the load.

Declare the design in the introduction. A sentence—“we do not test a pre-specified hypothesis; we document a pattern, enumerate the explanations consistent with it, and present evidence that discriminates among them”—costs nothing and prevents the paper from being evaluated against a template it is not using. Reviewers punish papers that appear to have failed at deduction far more than papers that never attempted it.

Keep the conventional headings and put PEEBI underneath them, as in the last column of Table 76.5. The structure is a reporting discipline, not a demand for new section names, and a manuscript that renames its sections after an epistemology spends its first reviewer paragraph defending a formatting choice.

State the ceiling before a reviewer does. The abductive paper’s ceiling is that \(\mathcal{E}\) may be incomplete, and the correct response is to say so and to name what evidence would change the ranking. Papers that specify the observation that would overturn their preferred explanation read as confident; papers that imply the candidate set is exhaustive read as naive. This is the same principle that governs the R&R response in Chapter 77—make the reader’s job of disagreeing with you easy, and they will usually decline the invitation.

Figure 76.2 summarizes the flow, including the loop that the deductive template has no way to represent: evaluation frequently sends the author back for more candidates or more context, and the paper reports the end state of that loop rather than pretending it did not run.

76.4.7 A checklist for the abductive manuscript

A reader finishing each act should be able to answer one question. If they cannot, the act is not written yet.

  • After P: what did we believe before, and why is the observation surprising against that belief?
  • After E (establish): is the pattern real—measured how, in what population, and robust to what obvious artifacts?
  • After E (evaluate): what else could produce this pattern, and what does the evidence say about each of those?
  • After B: why this explanation rather than the runner-up, and what would change my mind?
  • After I: what claim travels beyond this setting, and where does it stop?

The parallel exercise for a course is worth assigning directly: take a published hypo-deductive paper in the student’s area, reconstruct the abductive history that almost certainly produced it, and rewrite the introduction in PEEBI form. Students discover quickly that the reconstructed version is both more honest and easier to read, which is the argument of Pillai et al. (2026) in miniature. The seminar treatment of abduction as a mode of inference, alongside empirical generalizations and stylized facts, is in Section 65.6.

76.5 The Decomposition Paper

A third genre sits beside description and abduction, and it is the one most likely to rescue a paper whose headline effect is small, imprecise, or already known. Its claim is not “\(X\) affects \(Y\)” but “\(X\) affects \(Y\) through these specific channels, which push in opposite directions, in these proportions, under these conditions.” The increment \(\Delta\mathcal{K}\) is the anatomy of an effect rather than its sign.

The genre is worth naming because the alternative is so common and so weak. A great many papers—in marketing, economics, and management alike—end at a signed average: the promotion raised sales, the technology cut employment, the entry helped the incumbent. Signed averages age badly. They do not transfer to settings where the mixture of channels differs, they cannot explain why two credible studies disagree, and they give a manager or regulator nothing to act on beyond “more” or “less.”

The exemplar. Clemens and Lewis (2026) study a question with a long history of irreconcilable estimates: does employing low-skill immigrants displace native workers? The design is a natural firm-level randomization—the US H-2B visa quota is allocated in part by federal lottery—paired with a pre-analysis plan and a purpose-built firm survey of 2021 lottery winners and losers. That alone would produce a signed average. What makes the paper a template is that the signed average is derived rather than reported.

The authors write down a monopolistically competitive firm producing with immigrant labor \(I\), native low-skill labor \(N\), capital \(K\), and high-skill labor \(H\) in a nested CES technology (Ottaviano and Peri 2012), facing demand elasticity \(\eta\), with immigrant–native substitution elasticity \(\sigma\). Two mechanisms then run in opposite directions. Substitution: immigrants and natives compete for the same tasks, so cheap access to one displaces the other, and the force is governed by \(\sigma\). Scale: relaxing the hiring constraint lets the firm expand output, raising demand for every input including native labor, and the force is governed by \(\eta\). Stripping the model to labor alone makes the arithmetic transparent: with \(s_I\) and \(s_N\) the immigrant and native revenue shares, the effects of winning the lottery on revenue and on native employment are \[ \ln\frac{R_w}{R_\ell} \approx s_I \cdot \frac{\eta - 1}{(\eta-1)(1-s_N) + (\sigma-1)s_N}\cdot \ln\frac{I_w}{I_\ell}, \qquad \ln\frac{N_w}{N_\ell} \approx s_I \cdot \frac{\eta - \sigma}{(\eta-1)(1-s_N) + (\sigma-1)s_N}\cdot \ln\frac{I_w}{I_\ell}. \tag{76.4}\]

The revenue effect is unambiguously non-negative. The employment effect has indeterminate sign, positive when \(\eta > \sigma\) and negative otherwise: whether immigrant hiring crowds natives in or out is not a fact about immigrants but a race between two elasticities. (With capital and high-skill labor restored, the crossing condition generalizes but keeps the same structure.)

Code
# Effects of an exogenous increase in immigrant employment, from eq-sw-decomp.
s_I <- 0.20; s_N <- 0.65          # revenue shares of immigrant and native labor
grid <- expand.grid(eta = c(4, 8, 16), sigma = c(0.5, 1.5, 3, 6))

denom <- with(grid, (eta - 1) * (1 - s_N) + (sigma - 1) * s_N)
grid$revenue_effect  <- with(grid, s_I * (eta - 1)     / denom)
grid$native_effect   <- with(grid, s_I * (eta - sigma) / denom)
grid$verdict <- ifelse(grid$native_effect > 0, "crowds in", "crowds out")

round_df <- within(grid, {
  revenue_effect <- round(revenue_effect, 3)
  native_effect  <- round(native_effect, 3)
})
round_df[order(round_df$eta, round_df$sigma), ]
#>    eta sigma revenue_effect native_effect    verdict
#> 1    4   0.5          0.828         0.966  crowds in
#> 4    4   1.5          0.436         0.364  crowds in
#> 7    4   3.0          0.255         0.085  crowds in
#> 10   4   6.0          0.140        -0.093 crowds out
#> 2    8   0.5          0.659         0.706  crowds in
#> 5    8   1.5          0.505         0.468  crowds in
#> 8    8   3.0          0.373         0.267  crowds in
#> 11   8   6.0          0.246         0.070  crowds in
#> 3   16   0.5          0.609         0.629  crowds in
#> 6   16   1.5          0.538         0.520  crowds in
#> 9   16   3.0          0.458         0.397  crowds in
#> 12  16   6.0          0.353         0.235  crowds in

Every row has a positive revenue effect; the native-employment column flips sign inside the same table. That single display carries more transferable knowledge than any average treatment effect estimated from it, because a reader in a different industry can locate their own \((\eta, \sigma)\) and read off the prediction. The paper’s empirical estimates then close the loop: losing the lottery cuts immigrant employment by 56% and contracts the firm—revenue elasticity about \(+0.16\), investment about \(+1.03\) in the working-paper version, with the published estimates in the range \(0.20\)–\(0.22\) for production and \(1.5\)–\(2.1\) for investment—while the effect on US employment is zero or positive. Read through Equation 76.4, a null employment effect is not a non-result: it identifies the substitution elasticity, which the authors back out at \(0.8\)–\(2.2\), low relative to the demand elasticity, which is exactly why scale wins.

The four moves worth stealing. The genre has a recognizable structure, and each move is portable to a marketing paper.

  1. Write the model that makes the sign ambiguous. The theory’s job here is not to generate a directional hypothesis but to prove that direction cannot be signed a priori. That reframes a null or mixed result from a failure into an estimate of the parameter that decides the race.
  2. Turn the mechanism into a prespecified heterogeneity test. The same model predicts where each channel should dominate—larger revenue effects for small firms facing more elastic demand, larger native-employment effects in rural areas where complementary workers have worse outside options—and both predictions were registered in advance and confirmed. Heterogeneity chosen after the fact is fishing; heterogeneity implied by the decomposition is a test.
  3. Recover the structural parameter from the reduced form. The reduced-form coefficients are used to invert for \(\sigma\), which is the quantity other studies argue about and the quantity that transfers.
  4. Say which quantity you estimated. The authors distinguish the LATE recovered from the usual shift-share instruments—variation in immigrant supply, irrespective of current demand—from the policy-relevant treatment effect of a policy-induced restriction, and argue their lottery identifies the latter. Naming the estimand is itself a contribution when the literature has been silently averaging over several.

Companion designs. The decomposition move is not foreign to marketing; it is simply underused as an explicit frame.

  • Promotion analytics has run on decomposition for decades: a sales spike splits into brand switching, category expansion, purchase acceleration, and stockpiling, and the split—not the spike—determines incremental profit (Van Heerde, Helsen, and Dekimpe 2007; Guyt and Gijsbrechts 2014) (Chapter 21).
  • Biswas, Yoganarasimhan, and Zhang (2026) decompose the value of channel adoption by the pathway that produced it, isolating forward buying from habit persistence, and show the two mechanisms imply opposite corrections to incremental CLV (Section 16.8).
  • Q. Liu et al. (2026) decompose the environmental effect of platform entry by market structure, finding that the entire average effect comes from dual-platform cities and none from single-platform ones (Section 70.7.1).
  • Ellickson, Kar, and Reeder (2023) decompose a campaign’s effect into the effects of its components with double machine learning, turning “the email worked” into which element of the email worked.
  • In economics, the same instinct underwrites the task-based decomposition of automation into displacement and reinstatement effects, and the decomposition of trade shocks into substitution and scale channels; the shared feature is that the aggregate is written as a sum of forces with known signs before it is estimated.

A field-experiment specimen. The decomposition frame suits a firm-run randomized experiment especially well, because a policy change seldom moves only one line of the profit statement. Fang et al. (2026) worked with a leading global e-commerce platform to test an agentic-AI refund policy on nearly one million customers. In the treatment arm, an AI system evaluated the customer’s multimodal evidence and offered a partial refund with no return required. The control arm kept the standard process: ship the item back for a full refund. No one could sign the net effect in advance, because the components push in different directions. Refund payouts can rise. Processing costs fall. Less hassle can raise long-run customer value. Strategic claiming is a cost. The paper’s economic framework writes the platform’s payoff in terms of these drivers and states the conditions under which the policy creates value. The experiment then signs each one: payouts rise, processing costs fall, long-term customer value rises, and the net effect on profit is positive. Treated customers go on to buy more, but they also show signs of strategic behavior. The case adds two moves to the four above.

  1. Name the bundle. The two arms differ in who decides (an AI agent or the standard process), in whether the item comes back, and in how much is refunded. The experiment identifies the effect of that policy as it would be deployed, not the effect of any one component, and the deployment effect is the quantity a platform deciding whether to deploy actually needs (Section 44.3.3). A reader who wants the separate effect of returnlessness needs a different design, and saying so up front pre-empts the referee who would otherwise ask for it.
  2. Measure the downside. Strategic behavior is the obvious objection to paying refunds without a return. Measuring it and pricing it into the net effect turns the referee’s first question into one of the paper’s findings.

The abstract is also a compact template for the genre. In order, it states the cost the status quo imposes, on consumers in hassle and on firms in money; the technology that makes a new policy feasible; the partner, the randomization, and the scale; the two arms, each described as a complete policy; the framework; the sign of each payoff component; the net effect; the countervailing risk; and the claim to novelty, here “one of the first large-scale causal evaluations” of agentic AI in customer service. The whole promise–payoff loop of Figure 76.1, from problem to redeemed claim, fits in fewer than two hundred words. (Only the abstract was accessible when this section was written; the design details and effect sizes are in the paper.)

Where it fails. Two failure modes recur. The first is decomposition by regression mediation with no design behind it: adding a mediator to a regression and reporting an “indirect effect” decomposes nothing if the mediator is endogenous, and this remains the most common way marketing papers claim mechanism without earning it. The second is decomposing into channels the data cannot separate; if two mechanisms imply identical predictions in every observable dimension, naming them both is rhetoric, not evidence. The test to apply before writing is simple: for each channel in the decomposition, state the observation that would change its estimated share. If no such observation exists, the channel is not identified and the decomposition should be presented as an interpretation rather than a result.

76.6 The Effect–Mechanism–Boundary Paper

A fourth architecture is now common enough in empirical strategy, marketing, and information systems to be worth naming, because students imitate its surface without understanding why it holds together. The paper establishes an effect, then explains it, then bounds it—three stages that answer, in order, whether, how, and for whom. Singh et al. (2026) is a well-built specimen and the running example here; its substance is discussed in Chapter 28.

Stage 1 establishes the effect. Firms adopting open-source product development gained 4–5% in gross margin, estimated with staggered difference-in-differences and replicated under a second DID estimator, generalized synthetic control, an instrumental variable, and two dynamic panel estimators (Chapter 44).

Stage 2 explains it. A moderated mediation model routes the effect through labor productivity and shows the pathway is switched on by external contributor participation (Section 44.9.6).

Stage 3 bounds it. A configurational analysis identifies the resource profiles under which the gains actually appear, finding R&D intensity in every high-profitability configuration (Section 42.2).

A different, equally instructive pairing is the multimethod paper in which one method produces the measure the other estimates. Huang, Huang, and Hong (2026) use machine learning to classify roughly 280,000 GitHub issues as maintenance or development work and then estimate, with econometrics, how two forms of workflow automation change resolution speed for each (Section 28.7.5). The writing lesson is that the two methods are not parallel robustness checks but a pipeline, so the paper must justify the classifier’s validity before the regression is believed, because any classification error enters the econometric stage as measurement error in the outcome’s category. The theory does the matching work: two mechanisms (mechanization, orchestration) are mapped to two innovation types (exploitative, explorative) before any data appear, so each estimate answers a stated prediction instead of fishing across cells.

76.6.1 Why the stages are ordered, and why the method changes

The ordering is not stylistic. Each stage exists to answer the objection the previous one provokes, which is the same architectural logic as the five-move template in Section 75.3. A reader shown a 4–5% margin gain immediately asks through what, and a reader given a mediation pathway immediately asks for which firms. Reversing the order strands the reader: a mechanism for an effect not yet established is a story about nothing, and a boundary condition on an unexplained effect is a subgroup table.

The subtler point, and the one students miss, is that the method changes at every stage because the question changes. Quasi-experimental estimators answer a counterfactual question about an average. Structural equation modeling answers a question about a pathway’s composition. Set-theoretic analysis answers a question about which combinations of conditions travel with the outcome. Running one technique through all three stages is a category error—a mediation model cannot establish an average effect against selection, and a difference-in-differences cannot represent equifinality. When a manuscript uses the same estimator throughout and merely adds interaction terms, it usually has one stage wearing three hats.

Robustness follows the same principle: put it where the identification is weakest. Their Stage 1 carries six estimators because that is where the causal claim lives. Stage 2 gets a base-versus-full model comparison on AIC and BIC, a 5,000-replication bootstrap, and a second operationalization of the moderator. Stage 3 gets consistency thresholds and a separate analysis of the negated outcome. A uniform robustness appendix applied indiscriminately to all three signals that the author has not thought about which claim is actually fragile.

76.6.2 The honesty requirement

The architecture has a built-in temptation, and resisting it is what separates the good version from the imitation. Identification strength declines across the stages. Stage 1 can be genuinely causal. Stage 2’s mediator-to-outcome link usually is not, because nothing randomized the mediator (Section 44.9.2). Stage 3 is set-theoretic description within a sample. A paper that presents all three in the same confident register is overclaiming, and a careful referee will say so. The fix costs one sentence per stage, stating what the design does and does not support, and it buys the credibility the rest of the paper spends.

Is your Stage 2 load-bearing?

The diagnostic for whether the later stages are contributions or decoration: would a null there have changed the paper? In the running example it would. Without the mediation result, the 4–5% is a fact with no account of itself, equally consistent with cost arbitrage—firms getting free labor—which the authors explicitly rule out by showing that value accrues to firms with R&D rather than to firms with low internal capacity. Without the configurational stage, the paper would recommend open source to everyone, and its actual finding is that it pays only for firms able to absorb what the community sends. If you cannot say what a null at Stage 2 or 3 would have meant, those stages are robustness checks with ambitions, and a referee will read them that way.

When adapting this architecture, the marketing translation is usually straightforward: an adoption or policy shock supplies Stage 1, a mediator the field already measures well—satisfaction, salience, search effort, salesforce productivity—supplies Stage 2, and the firm or customer heterogeneity the field argues about supplies Stage 3. The binding constraint is almost always Stage 2, because the mediator must be measured on the same units and at a frequency that lets it sit causally between the shock and the outcome.

76.6.3 A Second Specimen: When the Effect Is Already in Print

Chan et al. (2026), published online in JMR in 2026, uses the same three-stage architecture under a harder starting condition, and the contrast with the running example is instructive. Its question is whether a public EV charging station on a supermarket’s parking lot raises the store’s revenue; the substance is in Section 54.6.1. The difficulty is that two earlier studies had already reported that nearby chargers raise customer spending at US businesses, by about 5% and 3.2% (Babar and Burtch 2024; Zheng et al. 2024), so the Stage 1 estimate of 3.4% could not by itself be the contribution. This is the situation Section 76.5 describes, a headline effect that is already known, and the paper is worth reading for how its front end converts that effect into a contribution a marketing journal would publish.

The funnel earns the question before it reaches the literature. The introduction opens on the retailer’s opportunity rather than on energy policy: parking lots could become charging hubs that relieve drivers’ “charger anxiety”, and the habitual, high-frequency nature of grocery trips lines up with the recurring need to recharge. A second paragraph shows practice moving, with European grocers and Walmart installing chargers, and a third supplies the tension: penetration is still low, the grid and permitting constraints behind the slow rollout are expected to ease, and no one knows whether demand will materialize or through what mechanisms. The fourth paragraph makes the move that turns this into a marketing paper. It sets aside the rent or revenue share a retailer can earn from the charging operator and declares the grocer’s focal interest to be its core business; the data section later keeps charging income out of the revenue measure, so the dependent variable matches the question. The same paragraph discounts the existing evidence on grounds of credibility rather than absence: industry reports that chargers lift sales lack causal identification, often come from parties with a stake in the answer, and say nothing about mechanisms or boundary conditions. Only then come the three research questions (effect, process, boundary conditions), one paragraph of data and design, and three contributions that mirror the questions one for one. Each contribution closes by naming who can act on it: retailers and policymakers for the effect size, store managers for the process evidence, and managers rolling chargers out across a chain for the heterogeneity. The abstract ends the same way. Figure 76.3 traces the chain.

Positioning against two predecessors is done in a table. The literature section grants the economics, transportation, and operations streams their own questions (subsidies, optimal charger placement, the incentives of businesses to host chargers) and narrows to the one that is open for a retailer: what hosting does to store performance. The two predecessors are credited with showing that a positive effect is possible, and a positioning table then lists study characteristics, process analyses, and heterogeneity analyses as rows, with check marks showing where each earlier study overlaps. That table is \(\mathcal{K}_{\text{before}}\) made explicit, the remedy for the annotated bibliography described in Section 76.14. Each empirical difference is tied to a specific weakness rather than asserted as better data. Cross-sector averages may hide sector heterogeneity, so the paper studies one sector to gain internal validity. Third-party card data omit cash, and cashless payment is known to raise spending, so retailer revenue including cash removes a possible bias. Foot-traffic counts include people who buy nothing, so actual transactions replace them. Chargers anywhere nearby give way to chargers on the retailer’s own premises, which is what a retailer controls. Germany complements the US evidence, and a staggered-robust estimator replaces two-way fixed effects. The substantive gap is then grounded in what the earlier data structurally could not show (a footnote notes they had no within-store variation across categories), and the paper quotes each predecessor’s own call for future research, one for sales measured directly at the retailer and one for the underlying causes of the spending effect, before stating that it answers both.

The identification story is institutional first and tested second. The case for exogenous timing comes from how chargers actually get built. The retailer’s management explains that hardware shortages, grid capacity, and permits from several parties make the go-live date unpredictable by anywhere from a few months to more than a year, and operators racing to sign partnerships are not timing individual stores. The authors then call their own approach conservative and test each way the claim could fail: model-free before-and-after evidence first, then conditional parallel trends, pre-trend leads, selection on observables, late adopters as controls, timing regressed on store traits, a stacked synthetic-control design, alternative catchments and distance thresholds, and named confounds (click and collect, pricing) checked one at a time.

Stage 2 is built by decomposing the outcome, not by adding a mediator. This is the sharpest contrast with the running example and a direct answer to the binding constraint just named. Rather than measure a mediator, the paper splits the outcome along its own identity (revenue is transactions times average basket) and reruns the Stage 1 design on each piece, then on transactions by weekday or weekend and peak or off-peak hour, on promoted versus non-promoted sales, and on dozens of food categories. Two further tests apply the same design to new contrasts: chargers equally close but off the store’s lot, and chargers added by a nearby rival, observed through the chain’s untreated stores. Because each of these tests inherits the Stage 1 identification, most of Stage 2 keeps the causal register that the honesty requirement says mediation usually loses. The exception is the last step, which regresses the category-level effects on category traits such as impulse buying and ability to stockpile; that is association across categories, and it should be read as such. What the decomposition delivers is concrete: more transactions, unchanged basket size, and the largest gains in weekend off-peak hours.

Stage 3 reports the difference test, not just two subgroup estimates. For every median split the paper reports whether the two subgroup effects differ, and several do not (absolute store size, distance to a main road, local charger density), which the text states plainly; the euro translations in the appendix are restricted to splits whose subgroups differ significantly. The register is less even between results and summary. The market-stealing test yields ATT \(= -0.0180\) (\(p = 0.067\)), and the authors note that their data cannot quantify how much of the treated stores’ gain came from rivals; the abstract nonetheless reports “significant evidence for market stealing”, and the discussion says stealing contributes substantially. A reader who checks the summary sentence against the table will notice the difference, and so will a referee. The qualifier the table carries belongs in the sentence that summarizes it.

The “so what” is priced in the reader’s currency. The 3.4% becomes roughly €200,000 a year for an average store. The discussion frames a “triple dividend”: rent from the operator, a higher top line, and demand spread more evenly across the week, which eases staffing. A null result, that a category’s environmental footprint does not predict its uplift, is reported as a finding against an intuitive expectation. The research implications place the paper in three marketing conversations: retail performance, keeping physical stores relevant, and sustainability-oriented marketing. The published version also carries an approved alternative disclosure plan, with proprietary data and disguised data and code deposited with the journal’s Data Editor, which is how a paper built on one retailer’s books meets JMR’s replication policy.

Arguing for an effect someone else found first
  1. Name the decision maker whose question this is, and choose the outcome that answers that question, even if it means excluding revenue the treatment also produces.
  2. Treat earlier estimates as a baseline to sharpen. Tie each design difference to a specific bias or blind spot in the earlier measures, never to “better data” in general.
  3. Ground the gap in what earlier data could not show, and quote the earlier authors’ own calls for future research when they exist.
  4. Put the positioning in a table a reviewer can audit at a glance.
  5. Argue exogeneity from the process that sets the treatment date, then test each way that argument could fail.
  6. If no mediator is measured on the right units at the right frequency, decompose the outcome and rerun the Stage 1 design on each component.
  7. Report the difference test for every split, and keep the summary sentence in the same register as the table behind it.
  8. End each contribution with the person who can act on it, and price it in that person’s currency.

76.6.4 A Third Specimen: Mechanism by Moderation, Without a Model

Luca, Nagaraj, and Subramani (2026), published in Management Science in 2026 (marketing department), ask whether being listed on a review platform raises a small business’s revenue. Their answer is 5% to 10% for Texas bars and restaurants added to Yelp. The paper is worth studying for its craft more than its topic. It builds all three stages from reduced-form evidence, with no structural demand model and no formal theory model. It also runs on an outcome anyone can download (Section 33.8). The account below draws its numbers from the NBER working-paper version (Luca, Nagaraj, and Subramani 2022). The heterogeneity results summarized at the end are from the published abstract, because the working paper does not yet contain them.

The main effect is set up by a descriptive puzzle. The paper’s first result is a count, not a coefficient. About 18% of alcohol-serving establishments in the state still had no listing at the end of 2017, and 4,810 of 14,381 were never listed at all, even though a listing costs nothing. That fact does two jobs. It makes the causal question non-obvious: if a free listing raised revenue, why would so many owners skip it? It also sets the extensive margin apart from the review literature, which had studied ratings, rankings, and review counts for businesses already on the platform. The working paper then gives the magnitude a familiar benchmark, comparing it with the revenue value of one additional star.

The endogeneity argument is a ladder, and each rung removes the owner from the timing decision. The threat is specific: an owner might add a listing during a renovation, an ownership change, or an upswing, and the revenue gain would then belong to those events. The paper answers with four samples, each estimated with the same imputation difference-in-differences and establishment and county-by-month fixed effects (Figure 76.4). The estimate is 0.052 log points for all listings and 0.052 for venues listed at least three months after opening, which rules out a new-venue ramp-up. It is 0.089 for the 747 venues listed by 56 “super-adders”, the top 1% of users by listings created, whose timing has nothing to do with the restaurant’s plans. It is 0.104 for the 1,295 venues Yelp created on 22 and 23 July 2010 from a purchased directory file, whose timing the platform set. The direction of travel is the argument. If owner timing inflated the full-sample estimate, taking the owner out should shrink it. It grows instead. Event-study leads close the case by showing no rise in revenue before any listing.

Two qualifications show what each rung costs. First, every rung changes the population as well as the identification. Bulk-added venues are more rural (75% urban against 86% for all listed venues) and later earn a mean rating of 2.09 against 3.03. So the 0.104 is an effect for the kind of venue that waits to be added, not a cleaner estimate of the 0.052. The ladder supports “positive, and not an artifact of owner timing”. It does not support a single number. Second, the estimator is part of the evidence. Ordinary two-way fixed effects give 0.054 for the bulk sample, about half the two-stage estimate. The paper explains its choice by its setting: the panel is unbalanced in calendar time, and Yelp’s reach grows over the sample, so effects should differ by when a venue was listed. That is the case in which the robust estimators of Section 44.1.6 matter. The two-way results go in an appendix, so a reader can see the gap.

Measurement is validated where it could fail. Two of the paper’s inputs are proxies, and each gets its own check. Alcohol receipts stand in for total revenue, and an appendix assembles outside evidence that the two move together. The tax-to-Yelp match comes from Yelp’s internal matcher, which the authors audited with three crowdworkers per venue on 750 venues. Of the matched venues, 241 of 250 really were on Yelp. Of the unmatched venues, 202 of 250 really were absent. The second number deserves more weight than the working paper gives it. The paper says only false positives affect its regressions, but never-listed venues are its main control group. A listed venue misclassified as unlisted therefore sits among the controls, and with about one unmatched venue in five actually listed, the bias runs toward zero.

The mechanism comes from who gains, not from a mediator. The first specimen measured a mediator, and the second decomposed the outcome. This paper takes a third route, and it is the one open to anyone without a mediator series. Each candidate mechanism predicts which venues should gain more. If a listing works by standing in for reputation the venue cannot build otherwise, gains should be larger where reputation is hard to build: independents rather than chains, and tourist areas whose customers lack local knowledge. If a listing works by revealing quality to people who would not otherwise see it, gains should be larger for better products. The published abstract reports both patterns. Independents and venues in tourist areas gain more, and so do larger venues and those with good reviews. Each split is a prediction stated before the table, so the heterogeneity table is the mechanism test. A disclosure result answers the opening puzzle. Venues that stayed off the platform until the bulk import earned lower ratings, as voluntary-disclosure models predict: owners who expect bad reviews have a reason not to list. Even so, they gained from being listed.

The honesty requirement applies with full force here, because no one randomized chain status. A chain-versus-independent split is also a split by size, location, and management. Moderation evidence is consistent with a mechanism. It does not isolate one. Its strongest form, which this design reaches toward, pairs splits on which rival mechanisms predict opposite signs, so that only one story fits the whole pattern.

Explaining an effect without a model
  1. Open with the descriptive fact that makes the causal question puzzling (here, free listings that many owners skip).
  2. Name who chooses the treatment date, and build a ladder of samples in which someone progressively further from the outcome chooses it.
  3. Read the ladder by the direction its estimates move, and say what population each rung represents.
  4. Justify the estimator from features of the setting (unbalanced panel, effects that grow with the platform), and show the naive estimator in an appendix.
  5. Audit every constructed variable, and work out which group each error type contaminates.
  6. Derive from each candidate mechanism a prediction about who gains more, state it before the table, and treat the heterogeneity table as the mechanism test.
  7. Use the selection result (who stayed out) to answer the puzzle you opened with.

The template transfers directly to studies of firms adopting a free digital channel, such as opening a social media account, joining a marketplace, or claiming a profile. Each shares the three problems this paper solves. The adopter picks the date, the non-adopters are a selected group worth describing in their own right, and the outcome has to come from outside the platform, or the effect of being on the platform is measured with the platform’s own data. The rung to look for is an adoption whose date someone other than the firm set. Tax receipts, permits, and other administrative records solve the outcome problem when they exist, and Section 33.8 shows what one such source takes to use.

76.6.5 A Fourth Specimen: A Small Reward Framed as Four Open Questions

Bruers, Ooghe, and Schokkaert (2026), published online in Management Science in 2026, is about as plain as a field experiment gets. Four of twelve Red Cross-Flanders donation centers gave plasma donors one extra thank-you coupon, worth about €1.50, for six months. There is no structural model, no instrument, and no machine learning. The paper is worth reading for how a modest manipulation became a contribution a general-interest journal would take. It fits the three-stage architecture loosely. There is a randomized effect, boundaries in time and across behaviors, and a mechanism stage built from a survey. Published estimates below come from the article’s abstract. Design details and month-by-month estimates come from the KU Leuven dissertation chapter that first reported the experiment (Bruers 2024).
