Where the two versions differ, we say so.

One experiment, four questions. The dissertation chapter asked a collector’s question: how cost-effective are small material rewards for plasma donors? The published version asks four questions about prosocial behavior in general. Each is answered by a single feature of the design (Table 76.7). This is the move most worth copying. A narrower paper would bury the information-only arm, the month-by-month estimates, and the blood-donation outcome as robustness checks. Here each becomes a headline result, because each answers a question the literature had left open.

Each question also passes the test of Section 76.2.3: both answers would have been publishable. A null on the first question would be evidence of crowding-out. A drop below baseline after the coupon was withdrawn would have been a backlash result. Zero substitution would mean the gain was net. The paper did not need any particular sign to have a contribution, which is what made a small experiment safe to run for two years.

The long panel turns a small effect into a dynamics story. Figure 76.5 shows the schedule. The reward arm received the newsletter item for three months before its extra coupon began, to accustom donors to seeing the coupons stated. Every change was announced a month ahead. That staggering separates the reminder from the reward within a single arm. The dissertation’s monthly estimates trace the shape. The reward effect climbs from 6.4% in January 2023 to 9.8% in June. The information effect peaks at about 8% in the second and third months and falls to 0.8% by the ninth. The versions disagree on one point. The dissertation reports a 4.4% effect in the first month after withdrawal, which then fades. The published abstract says the effect disappears immediately. Quote the version you cite.

The dissertation’s appendix prints the monthly donation counts for each center, so the picture can be redrawn from the page. Figure 76.6 redraws it and fits the dissertation’s center-level robustness model: log monthly donations on center and month fixed effects plus the two treatment indicators.

Code
# Monthly plasma donations at the 12 Red Cross-Flanders donation centers,
# November 2021 to October 2023, transcribed from Table 88 of the dissertation
# chapter that reports the experiment (Bruers 2024).
centers <- c("Aalst", "Brugge", "Edegem", "Geel",               # control
             "Genk", "Gent", "Mechelen", "Roeselare",           # information
             "Kortrijk", "Sint-Niklaas", "Turnhout", "Leuven")  # information + reward
arm <- rep(c("control", "information", "reward"), each = 4)
plasma <- matrix(c(
    625,  781, 1084,  493,  801, 1205,  570,  692,  945,  488,  535, 1274,  # Nov/21
    762, 1004, 1223,  681,  943, 1439,  746,  853, 1128,  647,  690, 1397,  # Dec/21
    734,  831, 1127,  592,  806, 1108,  686,  799,  971,  567,  654, 1129,  # Jan/22
    747,  901, 1122,  628,  849, 1259,  667,  753,  971,  561,  605, 1333,  # Feb/22
    725,  942, 1201,  707,  822, 1339,  690,  859, 1033,  614,  658, 1368,  # Mar/22
    606,  754,  955,  572,  717, 1106,  572,  674,  947,  514,  534, 1137,  # Apr/22
    660,  888, 1125,  581,  819, 1327,  633,  718,  999,  517,  572, 1340,  # May/22
    724,  873, 1148,  585,  868, 1242,  588,  812, 1068,  653,  645, 1306,  # Jun/22
    768,  998, 1182,  698,  993, 1171,  825,  864, 1062,  639,  702, 1383,  # Jul/22
    937, 1217, 1481,  839, 1246, 1520,  963, 1032, 1271,  757,  808, 1637,  # Aug/22
    771, 1018, 1199,  763, 1034, 1394,  878,  974, 1203,  699,  760, 1517,  # Sep/22
    648,  793,  982,  612,  757, 1225,  629,  764,  904,  498,  630, 1278,  # Oct/22
    710,  791,  989,  559,  876, 1277,  656,  772,  986,  567,  583, 1319,  # Nov/22
    719,  825,  923,  573,  807, 1311,  614,  784,  980,  590,  632, 1337,  # Dec/22
    657,  785,  975,  616,  815, 1124,  666,  800, 1005,  534,  640, 1356,  # Jan/23
    589,  834,  920,  571,  790, 1222,  599,  745, 1025,  577,  601, 1301,  # Feb/23
    741,  889,  959,  637,  810, 1286,  702,  872, 1093,  661,  697, 1454,  # Mar/23
    624,  749,  831,  500,  675, 1110,  523,  735,  983,  508,  564, 1214,  # Apr/23
    661,  802,  914,  537,  731, 1138,  601,  740,  997,  513,  632, 1244,  # May/23
    610,  819,  907,  543,  727, 1115,  531,  769, 1030,  551,  609, 1187,  # Jun/23
    769,  991, 1202,  653,  888, 1291,  805,  927, 1201,  656,  752, 1373,  # Jul/23
    896, 1148, 1401,  831,  873, 1573,  938, 1087, 1352,  736,  845, 1613,  # Aug/23
    727,  909, 1000,  629,  778, 1286,  689,  887, 1072,  585,  739, 1191,  # Sep/23
    619,  817,  993,  575,  739, 1340,  630,  856, 1023,  575,  678, 1390   # Oct/23
  ), nrow = 24, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(NULL, centers))
month <- -10:13   # month 1 = October 2022, the first newsletter that states the coupons

# Each treated arm's total relative to the control arm, rescaled so that the
# eleven pre-experiment months average 1 (the dissertation's Figure 38).
arm_total <- sapply(split(seq_along(centers), arm), function(j) rowSums(plasma[, j]))
relative  <- arm_total[, c("information", "reward")] / arm_total[, "control"]
relative  <- sweep(relative, 2, colMeans(relative[month <= 0, ]), "/")

plot(month, relative[, "reward"], type = "n", ylim = c(0.93, 1.18),
     xlab = "Month (1 = October 2022)", ylab = "Plasma donations relative to control",
     main = "Information decays; the extra coupon builds, then stops")
rect(0.5, 0, 9.5, 2, col = "grey92", border = NA)   # newsletter states the coupons
rect(3.5, 0, 9.5, 2, col = "grey82", border = NA)   # reward arm: third coupon
abline(h = 1, lty = 3)
lines(month, relative[, "information"], type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 2)
lines(month, relative[, "reward"], type = "b", pch = 16)
legend("topleft", c("Information arm", "Information + reward arm"),
       pch = c(1, 16), lty = c(2, 1), bty = "n")

# The dissertation's center-level robustness model: log donations on center and
# month fixed effects plus the two treatment indicators.
d <- data.frame(month = rep(month, 12), center = rep(centers, each = 24),
                arm = rep(arm, each = 24), donations = as.vector(plasma))
d$information <- as.integer(d$arm != "control" & d$month %in% 1:9)
d$reward      <- as.integer(d$arm == "reward"  & d$month %in% 4:9)
fit <- lm(log(donations) ~ factor(month) + factor(center) + information + reward, data = d)
round(100 * (exp(coef(fit)[c("information", "reward")]) - 1), 1)   # percent effects
#> information      reward 
#>         3.6         6.0

Plain least squares on the transcribed table gives 3.6% for the information item and 6.0% for the reward. For this model the dissertation reports 3.3% and 5.5%, fitted with autocorrelated errors that we did not reproduce. Its preferred donor-level fixed-effects Poisson model gives 4.6% and 7.1%, the figures the published abstract carries. The figure also shows why the donor-level model carries the paper. With four centers per arm, the pre-period ratios wander by up to about five percent either side of 1. Month 0, before any treatment, already sits near 1.06 in both arms. The late spike in month 13 comes from a recruitment campaign, which the dissertation notes worked best at the two largest centers, both in treated arms.

Substitution is priced, not just reported. The partner collects blood and plasma at the same sites, so the experiment can see what the coupon costs in the prosocial act it did not reward. In the dissertation’s numbers, the blood decline is barely significant at the donor level (p = 0.047) and not significant in the center-level model. It accounts for about one sixth of the plasma gain. The paper reports it anyway, and the cost arithmetic shows why. Every plasma donor gets the extra coupon, including those who would have come anyway. The dissertation therefore puts the marginal cost at €1.50 × 107% / 7%, about €23 per extra plasma donation, and €34 once the lost blood donations are netted out. The same dissertation’s meta-analysis puts the cost of cash or vouchers worth €5 to €15 per blood donation at €20 to €120 per extra donation. A cost per net extra donation is the number a collector can act on.

The partner shapes the design, and the paper says how. The Red Cross funded the study and supplied administrative records on 77,646 donors who gave at a center at least once over the two years. The outcome is therefore a count of donations, not a stated intention. The partner’s rules also set the design’s limits. An informal cap of about €5 on rewards for voluntary, unpaid donation limited the reward to three coupons. A rule against treating donors at the same center differently meant that centers, not donors, were randomized. The twelve centers were grouped by cluster analysis into four triplets of similar size and donor mix, and one center per triplet went to each arm. Matching helps, but twelve units cannot balance everything: 43% of control-arm donors lived more than 15 km from their center, against 26% in each treated arm. Inference is the other cost. The dissertation clusters standard errors by donor, although treatment varies by center. With twelve clusters, a referee will ask for center-level inference such as the wild cluster bootstrap (Section 44.1.5). Say in the paper what the partner allowed and what it cost.

Registration, described accurately. The trial appears in the AEA RCT Registry (Bruers, Ooghe, and Schokkaert 2024), but the entry was submitted in August 2024, more than a year after the intervention ended in June 2023. The dissertation states that no preregistration was done, while noting that the models and hypotheses were fixed before data collection. A registration filed after the data exist documents a design. It does not constrain the analysis the way a pre-analysis plan does, and a careful reader will check the dates. Describe your own registration by its date.

A mechanism stage without a model. The dissertation closed by asking whether a larger reward works through donors’ self-interest or by signaling that donations are more urgently needed. The published version answers with survey evidence. Small rewards act as signals of increased need or as gifts that call for reciprocity, and the authors suggest the findings may carry over to volunteering. The survey’s design is not described in the versions we could read. Asking recipients how they interpret an incentive is a cheap mechanism stage, and the honesty requirement applies to it in full: stated interpretations are consistent with a mechanism but do not isolate one.

Making a small field experiment publishable
  1. Turn the one effect into several open questions, and give each a design feature that answers it.
  2. Write each question so that either answer is a result, including a null.
  3. Run the panel long enough to see build-up, decay, and what happens after the treatment ends, and report effects month by month.
  4. Measure the behavior the incentive might pull people away from, and fold the loss into the cost per unit gained.
  5. Give reminding people of what they already get its own arm, separate from giving them more.
  6. Use the partner’s administrative outcomes, and state which of the partner’s rules shaped the design.
  7. Match inference to the unit of randomization, and say how many clusters you have.
  8. Date your registration honestly, and add a direct check on mechanism, even a survey, before a referee asks for one.

The template carries over to loyalty programs and promotions. A points bonus on one product line is the same experiment, and substitution away from the other lines is the outcome that keeps the estimate honest.

76.6.6 A Fifth Specimen: One Effect, Several Routes

Agarwal et al. (2026), published in Management Science in 2026 (finance department), ask whether building a rural road brings a village’s households into the stock market. The treatment and the outcome sit far apart, and a reader’s first reaction is to ask how asphalt could open a brokerage account. That distance is why the paper is useful here. The main effect takes one table. Most of the paper is spent on the routes from road to trade, and each route gets its own prediction, its own data source, and its own test. The earlier specimens each explained an effect one way: a mediator, a decomposition, a moderator table, a survey. This one runs several explanations side by side and tries to discriminate among them.

The account below is drawn from the February 2022 working paper (Agarwal et al. 2022), because the published text was not accessible when this section was written. Where the published abstract differs, the difference is noted. Magnitudes need particular care. The February 2022 draft reports that a new road raises the number of new investors in a postal code by 28.7% and their trades by 64.5%. The abstract on record for the SSRN version reports 6.8% and 7.9%, and the published abstract reports no magnitude. The numbers below are the 2022 draft’s and show the pattern of the argument. Take magnitudes from the published tables before quoting any.

The setting supplies the design, and the paper borrows it openly. India’s rural road program (PMGSY) built all-weather feeder roads to more than 115,000 previously unconnected villages. Development economists had already used the program to study schooling, labor, and lending, and the paper says it follows the empirical strategy of one of those studies. The new ingredient is the outcome: every trade on the National Stock Exchange by 13.5 million individual investors, each tagged with a postal code. The authors assign villages to postal codes within five kilometers, keep the 4,154 postal codes that received their first program road between October 2004 and February 2015, and estimate a monthly panel with postal-code, month, and district-by-year fixed effects. Every unit is eventually treated, so the comparison is only ever about timing (Section 44.5 discusses what that costs). A new outcome on an accepted design is a legitimate contribution, and it leaves the referee’s attention for the mechanism sections, which is where this paper wants it.

The main effect is split once before any mechanism is discussed. New investors, defined as accounts less than three years old, drive most of the response. In the 2022 draft the effect is about six additional new investors and 214 additional trades per postal code per month, in a sample where the average postal code has 36 active investors. Effects are larger in rural postal codes and in areas of intermediate development. The poorest tenth by consumption shows no extra response relative to developed areas. That split is a boundary result and a first hint about mechanism. It is what one would expect if a road cannot create investors where there is little to invest.

Each route is written as a prediction about something other than the headline outcome. Figure 76.7 and Table 76.8 give the structure. The information route says a road lowers the cost of learning about stocks, through better access to facts about companies and through more contact with people who already invest (Hong, Kubik, and Stein 2004). If so, three things should follow, and none of them is the participation count. Remote places, where information was scarcest, should respond more. Portfolios should broaden. Holdings should reach toward firms farther away. The financial-inclusion route says a road brings bank branches, and a branch is where an account gets opened and where savings sit before they move. If so, the effect should concentrate in postal codes where a branch opened after the road, and money should leave savings deposits and consumption. A third candidate is a rival more than a route: roads raise incomes, and richer households buy stocks. If that were the whole story, the response should concentrate in months of good rainfall, the standard proxy for a positive income shock in rural India.

Every route costs a new dataset. The right-hand columns of Table 76.8 list a census, a firm database, a confidential branch register, deposit returns, a household survey, and a rainfall archive. Mechanism sections in student drafts usually re-cut the main regression by variables already in the file. Here each claim about a route is checked against a measurement that the main result did not use, which is why seven rows read as seven pieces of evidence and not one result shown seven ways.

The best split is the one on which two stories disagree. A branch could raise participation because households want to invest and now can, or because bank staff sell investments. The authors argue that state-owned banks reach further into rural areas but earn less fee income, and so have less reason to push stock trading. The demand story therefore predicts a stronger effect for state-owned branches, and the sales story a weaker one. The estimate is stronger for state-owned branches. This is the move the third specimen reached toward: a moderator chosen because rival accounts predict opposite signs. The published abstract adds a route the 2022 draft lacks, risk sharing, under which roads should matter more where incomes are volatile, and reports limited evidence for it. A route that was proposed, tested, and found weak is reported as such, and it makes the two surviving routes more credible.

The last stage qualifies the headline. Participation is usually treated as a good outcome, and the paper could have stopped there. It asks instead how the new investors did. In the 2022 draft, trades after road completion earn money over 1-day and 10-day holding periods, show no detectable profit over 25 days, and lose money over 140 trading days, and trading shifts toward more volatile stocks. The published abstract keeps the conclusion: infrastructure raises participation but not necessarily the quality of investment outcomes. This is a fourth stage beyond effect, mechanism, and boundary, and it changes the policy sentence. Without it the paper recommends roads as financial-inclusion policy. With it the paper says roads bring people in and something else has to help them invest well.

Where the specimen is thin. The honesty requirement of Section 76.6 applies, and a conference discussion of the working paper states the problem compactly (Hong 2022). A road moves everything at once: information, bank access, and income. If bank branches were treated as the variable of interest and the road as its instrument, the exclusion restriction would fail, because the road also works through the other routes. The branch split has a second weakness. A branch that opens after the road is itself an outcome of the road, and banks choose where to open, so the postal codes with new branches may be the ones where demand for investing was about to rise anyway. The discussion asks which way causation runs between branches and participation. The rainfall test addresses transitory income only, and a permanent rise in income from better market access remains a live alternative. The evidence supports “both routes are operating” and does not support a share for each. A paper that needs shares has to write down a model, as in Section 76.3.4, or find separate variation in each route. The same discussion suggests a different frame, the unplanned benefits of public-goods spending, which shows that the frame was a choice.

Explaining one effect through several routes
  1. Before any mechanism test, split the main effect on the margin that matters (here, new against experienced investors) so the reader knows whose behavior needs explaining.
  2. Write each route as a causal sentence, then derive an implication for a variable other than the headline outcome.
  3. Bring a new measurement to each implication. Re-cutting the main regression by variables already in the file is weaker evidence.
  4. Include the dull rival (people simply got richer) and give it a test of its own.
  5. Look for one split on which two versions of a route predict opposite signs.
  6. Report a route that found little support. It makes the others more credible.
  7. Say that the tests show which routes operate and do not apportion the effect among them, and flag any split that conditions on something the treatment itself caused.
  8. End by asking whether the outcome you raised was good for the people concerned, and let the answer change the policy sentence.

The template carries over to marketing questions where a distant cause is suspected of moving a consumer outcome: broadband rollout and online shopping, a new store format and category entry, a payment technology and spending. In each, the main effect is the short part of the paper, and the list of routes, with one outside dataset apiece, is the plan for the rest.

76.7 The Lifecycle Paper: How Response Changes Across Stages

Many marketing questions are really about a process. A product is announced, launched, reviewed, discounted, and retired. An event is advertised, held, and then sold as a recording. A customer searches, buys, uses, and complains. A lifecycle paper takes one response parameter, such as a price elasticity, an advertising effect, or the weight of word of mouth, and asks how it changes from stage to stage. The finding is the profile across stages, not a single number. Done well, the paper also says why the profile has that shape. The two usual reasons are that different people act at different stages, and that the same people know or want different things at different stages. Separating them is the core analytical task of the genre.

The genre borrows from its neighbors. Each stage needs a credible estimate, as in Section 76.6. The gap between stages is decomposed into selection and within-person change, as in Section 76.5. The mechanism is often tested by moderation, as in Section 76.6.4. What sets it apart is the axis everything is organized on: a sequence of stages whose boundaries are fixed by an institution rather than by the analyst.

The specimen. Cong, Liu, and Manchanda (2026) ask how demand for paid livestreams responds to price before the stream and after it, when the recording is on sale (Section 21.8.2 has the substance). On a Chinese knowledge-sharing platform, 2,299 talks sold at a price fixed for their whole life. Demand before the stream has an elasticity of about \(-1.2\), and demand for the recording about \(-0.8\). The paper traces the gap partly to who buys early (heavy users, who are more price-sensitive) and partly to what buyers know (quality is uncertain until the ratings arrive), and ends with stage-specific prices. The account below follows the authors’ June 2026 arXiv version, which carries the published title.

76.7.1 The moves worth copying

Let the institution define the stages. The stages here are set by the platform: the listing date, the stream, and the switch to recording. The analyst did not choose them after looking at the data. The paper’s first figure is the lifecycle itself, and the data section says what stays constant across stages. The price cannot change after listing, which is what makes a comparison of elasticities across stages meaningful. Events the platform discounted partway through are dropped for the same reason. The outcome windows (30 days on each side) are set so that stages are comparable across events, and the paper reports that they capture 85% of sales, so a reader can judge what was left out.

Test the gap, not two separate estimates. The main specification pools both stages and interacts price with a post-stream indicator, so the difference in elasticities has its own standard error. Separate regressions for each stage appear only as a robustness check. The authors justify this in a footnote, and it is worth copying. Note also what the pooled form buys for identification. If an omitted creator quality shifts demand equally in both stages, it biases the two elasticities by the same amount and leaves the gap unbiased. Saying this out loud tells a referee which claim is the robust one.

Describe who acts in each stage before modeling why. The first mechanism table is plain description: buyers before the stream have written more answers and have more followers than buyers of the recording. Only then does the paper estimate elasticities by buyer type. The order matters, because a selection story that has not first been shown in the raw composition reads as speculation.

Split the gap into selection and within-buyer change. The two explanations make different predictions. If the gap is pure selection, it vanishes once buyer type is held fixed. If buyers’ information changes, the gap survives within type. The paper runs this test twice: within engagement groups, and on the buyers who purchased in both stages, a group that holds composition fixed by construction. The gap survives both. A coarse proxy for type leaves some selection inside each group, so the within-type gap is an upper bound on within-buyer change. The simulation below shows why the test works.

Code
set.seed(2026)
J  <- 2000                                  # events, each sold before and after the stream
lp <- rnorm(J, log(20), 0.6)                # log price (RMB); fixed for the event's whole life
xi <- rnorm(J, 0, 0.5)                      # event appeal, independent of price here
eta <- c(frequent = 1.6, infrequent = 0.6)  # each type's price sensitivity

# Demand for event j in stage s from consumer type k is Poisson with mean
#   scale * share(k, s) * exp(xi_j - eta_ks * (lp_j - log 20)),
# where eta_ks = eta_k + shift if s is the pre-event stage (quality still uncertain).
simulate <- function(freq_pre, freq_post, shift_pre) {
  grid <- expand.grid(j = 1:J, stage = c("pre", "post"), type = names(eta),
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  share <- ifelse(grid$type == "frequent",
                  ifelse(grid$stage == "pre", freq_pre, freq_post),
                  ifelse(grid$stage == "pre", 1 - freq_pre, 1 - freq_post))
  e <- eta[grid$type] + ifelse(grid$stage == "pre", shift_pre, 0)
  grid$lp <- lp[grid$j]
  grid$q  <- rpois(nrow(grid), 400 * share * exp(xi[grid$j] - e * (grid$lp - log(20))))
  grid
}

# Elasticity in each stage from log(1 + demand) on log price, as in a stage-interacted model.
stage_elasticities <- function(d) {
  d$post <- as.integer(d$stage == "post")
  b <- coef(lm(log1p(q) ~ post * lp, data = d))
  c(pre = unname(b["lp"]), post = unname(b["lp"] + b["post:lp"]))
}
summarise <- function(d) {
  agg <- aggregate(q ~ j + stage + lp, data = d, FUN = sum)   # what the platform sees
  pooled <- stage_elasticities(agg)
  within <- sapply(names(eta), function(k) unname(diff(stage_elasticities(d[d$type == k, ]))))
  round(c(pre = pooled[["pre"]], post = pooled[["post"]],
          gap = pooled[["post"]] - pooled[["pre"]],
          gap_within_frequent = within[["frequent"]],
          gap_within_infrequent = within[["infrequent"]]), 2)
}

scenarios <- list(
  "Selection only"   = c(freq_pre = 0.8, freq_post = 0.2, shift_pre = 0),
  "Uncertainty only" = c(freq_pre = 0.5, freq_post = 0.5, shift_pre = 0.4),
  "Both"             = c(freq_pre = 0.8, freq_post = 0.2, shift_pre = 0.4)
)
res <- t(sapply(scenarios, function(p) summarise(do.call(simulate, as.list(p)))))
knitr::kable(res, col.names = c("Pre elasticity", "Post elasticity", "Gap (post - pre)",
                                "Gap within frequent", "Gap within infrequent"))
Pre elasticity Post elasticity Gap (post - pre) Gap within frequent Gap within infrequent
Selection only -1.41 -0.84 0.57 0.01 0.00
Uncertainty only -1.52 -1.13 0.39 0.39 0.39
Both -1.81 -0.84 0.96 0.41 0.40

In the first row, no buyer’s price sensitivity changes at all. Frequent, price-sensitive users simply make up 80% of the early market and 20% of the late one. The aggregate data still show demand that is far more elastic before the event (about \(-1.4\)) than after it (about \(-0.8\)), close to the pattern in the paper. Only the split by type gives it away: within each type the gap is zero. In the second row, the buyer mix is constant and every buyer becomes less price-sensitive once quality is known, so the gap appears both in aggregate and within each type. In the third row, both are at work and the aggregate gap is roughly their sum, while the within-type gap recovers the uncertainty part alone. This is the logic of the paper’s Table 10. The aggregate gap cannot tell the stories apart; the within-type gap can.

Test the within mechanism by where it should be weak. Quality uncertainty predicts a smaller gap wherever buyers already knew what they were getting: creators with a quality badge, “hard” topics whose quality can be judged from a description, and buyers who already followed the creator. Each prediction is stated before its table, and each holds. As in Section 76.6.4, moderation is consistent with the mechanism without isolating it, and the paper concedes that live and recorded content differ in other ways too.

Check that the boundary is not an artifact of the display. Platforms often show each stage differently. Here upcoming events sit at the top of the page and past events drift down it. If position drove the gap, elasticities would trend within each stage. Instead they are flat on both sides with a jump at the stream. The paper says plainly that it cannot rule out higher search costs for archived events. Naming the alternative you cannot exclude costs less credibility than letting a referee name it.

End with a policy and the assumption it rests on. The counterfactual compares one price for the whole life with a price for each stage, under linear demand and independent stages. The authors call the second assumption “admittedly strong” and name the dependence it ignores (cheap early tickets could cannibalize the recording or signal quality to its buyers). A lifecycle counterfactual almost always rests on some assumption about how stages are linked, so state it and say which way relaxing it would move the answer.

A lesson from the version history. The first public version (arXiv, July 2021) was titled “The Role of ‘Live’ in Livestreaming Markets.” It estimated a daily elasticity curve from two weeks before to two weeks after the stream with a generalized orthogonal random forest. Elasticity was about \(-0.5\) two weeks out, near zero on the stream day, and about \(-0.1\) afterward, and the paper attributed the stream-day pattern to the chance to interact with the creator in real time. The published paper (June 2026 arXiv) is plainer and stronger. The question became how demand changes across the lifecycle rather than what “live” is worth. The daily curve became a two-stage contrast with a pooled test and an instrument. The real-time interaction mechanism was dropped, because weekly elasticities in the run-up to the stream turned out to be flat. A self-selection mechanism and a pricing counterfactual were added. Coarser stages identified cleanly made a better paper than a fine-grained curve identified by a flexible method, and the mechanism the data no longer supported was cut rather than kept.

The genre in this book. Many papers already cited here have the same shape, and reading them as one genre makes the moves easier to see.

  • Elberse and Eliashberg (2003) model movies released in sequence across countries, where performance in the first market shapes demand and screen allocation in later ones.
  • Lehmann and Weinberg (2000) treat theatrical release and video as sequential channels and ask when the second stage should open, given that it cannibalizes the first.
  • Moe and Fader (2002) use advance purchase orders, the pre-release stage, to forecast sales after launch.
  • Y. Liu (2006) trace movie word of mouth from before release through the run and ask which features of it predict box office at each point.
  • Eliashberg et al. (2000) build a decision-support model for evaluating a movie before release.
  • Golder and Tellis (2004) explain the turning points of the product life cycle (takeoff and slowdown) with informational cascades.
  • Avery et al. (2012) show that the effect of opening stores on a retailer’s catalog and online channels changes with time since opening.
  • Lemon and Verhoef (2016) organize customer experience into pre-purchase, purchase, and post-purchase stages, the conceptual frame for journey papers.
  • Colicev, Kumar, and O’Connor (2019) link firm and user content to separate stages of the marketing funnel.
  • S. Y. Kim et al. (2026) ask whether a first customization experience changes the later stages of a customer’s journey, and separate who customizes from what customizing does with a randomized experience manipulation (Section 44.3.2).
  • Xie and Shugan (2001) give the theory for the stage before consumption, when buyers are uncertain about their own future state.
A checklist for writing your own lifecycle paper
  1. Define the stages by an event that changes what buyers know or who is buying (announcement, release, first reviews, the event itself, expiry), not by calendar time. Draw the lifecycle as the paper’s first figure.
  2. State what is held constant across stages (price, product, display) and drop units where the firm intervened partway through.
  3. Choose windows that make stages comparable across units, and report how much of total activity they capture.
  4. Estimate one pooled model with stage interactions so the gap has a standard error, and keep separate per-stage regressions as robustness.
  5. Identify the level of the parameter in every stage; then say which confounds the pooled form differences out of the gap.
  6. Show who acts in each stage with descriptive tables before proposing any mechanism.
  7. Split the gap into selection and within-buyer change: estimate by buyer type, and on buyers active in more than one stage. Report how much of the gap survives.
  8. For each within-buyer mechanism, name the units where it should be weak, state the prediction before the table, and test it.
  9. Check whether the stage boundary is an artifact of how the platform presents each stage: look for a jump at the boundary rather than a trend within stages.
  10. Turn the gap into a stage-specific policy, write down the assumption that links the stages (cannibalization, signaling, strategic waiting), and say which way relaxing it would move the answer.
  11. Bound the claim: one platform, one kind of content, one period.

76.8 The Field-Experiment Paper from an Emerging Market

A growing share of the data that marketing students hold comes from markets the field’s journals rarely see: a panel of retailers in Vietnam, a survey of vendors in Lagos, transaction logs from a network of mobile-money agents. Writing a paper from such data runs into a problem that none of the templates above solves on its own. The paper usually offers no new theory and no new method. Its evidence does not come as a list of hypotheses, each confirmed by a coefficient. What it has instead is a setting where an important question can be answered cleanly, and a design that answers it. Turning that into a paper takes craft. S. J. Anderson et al. (2026), published online in Marketing Science in October 2026, is a well-built specimen. It is a close cousin of the effect–mechanism–boundary paper (Section 76.6): a randomized experiment supplies the effect, and measured intermediate outcomes carry the mechanism.

(The published article was not accessible when this section was written. The publisher deposits a one-sentence abstract with Crossref. The fuller sources are the abstract of a 2022 working paper in the Private Enterprise Development in Low-Income Countries (PEDL) series, the abstract of a 2023 SSRN version, the trial’s entry in the AEA RCT Registry (AEARCTR-0005591), the article’s deposited reference list, and Chicago Booth Review coverage, including a 2024 article and a 2026 podcast interview with Chintagunta (Chicago Booth Review 2024, 2026). Each number below names the version it comes from. Where versions disagree, the text says so. The section structure discussed here is a reconstruction of what a paper in this genre must contain, not the article’s table of contents.)

76.8.1 The study in two paragraphs

The authors randomized 550 growth-oriented micro and small enterprises in Rwanda into three arms (registry). Two hundred fifty treatment firms received an Android smartphone, a data plan, and MARKETmanager, an app the researchers designed. Owners used it to record sales, products, customers, and marketing actions, and it returned monthly reports comparing the firm’s current performance with its past. Fifty placebo firms received the phone and data plan without the app. Two hundred fifty control firms received nothing during the study and were promised access afterward. The registry dates the intervention from July 2019 to March 2020. The 2022 working paper describes nine months of treatment, and the 2024 Booth Review article seven, ending as COVID-19 arrived. Staff visited treated owners to help them enter and read the data: weekly according to the registry, monthly according to the 2024 article. That article adds that the visitors explained the reports but gave no advice on what to do with them. In the podcast, Chintagunta describes the visitors as mostly undergraduates chosen for their lack of business experience.

The findings come in four families, listed in the same order in every version of the abstract. Usage started low and rose by the third month. The 2022 abstract reports daily usage rates of 90–95%. The 2024 article reports that about 30% of treated firms used the app daily at first, rising to 60%. The two figures probably measure different things, and only the paper can settle which. On mental performance, “objective ability and psychological tests” (six of them, according to the 2024 article) show gains in reasoning, memory, logic, and calculation. On practices, treated firms adopted product-management activities, with spillovers into accounting practices the app never targeted. On money, monthly sales were 36.4% and monthly profits 29.2% higher than in the control group on average. These two figures appear in the 2022, 2023, and published abstracts. The published abstract adds that comparisons with the placebo arm, which holds phone and internet access fixed, attribute the gains to the analytics rather than the device.

76.8.2 Where the contribution comes from without a new theory or method

A paper like this does not claim to have invented anything. Its contribution is one, or several, of three other kinds, and the specimen makes all three.

  1. A causal estimate of a quantity people already act on. Governments, donors, and software vendors already sell analytics to small firms on the assumption that it pays. The gap is not a missing theory but a missing number. The 2023 abstract says so in one line: analytics is “widely promoted”, but evidence on its effects for individual entrepreneurs “remains limited”. An evidence gap of this kind is legitimate when the quantity is policy-relevant and nobody has randomized it.
  2. A mechanism measured, not asserted. “Analytics improves decisions” is usually an assumption. Here it becomes an observation, because the authors tested the owners themselves. A battery of cognitive tests is a measurement contribution in a marketing journal, and it turns a firm-level result into a claim about people.
  3. A tension resolved. The 2022 abstract opens with two literatures that predict opposite signs. In one, technology builds the user’s human capital. In the other, analysis paralysis, confirmation bias, information overload, and “brain drain” erode it. The deposited reference list covers both: studies of cognitive training and neuroplasticity on one side, and on the other a 2025 experiment in which generative AI without guardrails harmed high-school students’ learning. A two-sided prior is what makes an empirical answer a contribution (Section 76.2.3). Neither side could have called the result in advance.

The contribution sentence of Section 76.2 adapts accordingly. It becomes: “We estimate the effect of [a treatment decision makers already buy or fund] on [the outcomes they care about] among [a population described by its economic role], a quantity prior work could not estimate because [the treatment is everywhere where data are rich, or nobody randomized it], and we show that the effect runs through [measured intermediate outcomes].”

The title history shows the same move. The 2022 working paper asked a question: “Is (Smart) Technology Really Making Us Dumber?” The 2023 SSRN version answered it: “(Smart) Technology Doesn’t Make Us Dumber”. The published title drops the provocation altogether: “From Data to Decisions: Marketing Analytics, Mental Performance, and Firm Growth in an Emerging Market”. It names the causal chain in order and puts the setting last, as a scope condition. The country does not appear in it at all.

76.8.3 The country as the source of variation, not a curiosity

The hardest sentence in an emerging-market paper answers the question a referee in Chicago or Rotterdam is silently asking: why should I care about Rwanda? The weak answer describes the country. The strong answer says what the country makes estimable. In rich markets almost every firm already has some data, so the value of analytics cannot be estimated from a starting point of none. In the specimen’s setting, few micro and small enterprises “formally record their marketing data” (registry). In the podcast, Chintagunta puts the baseline share with any records at about 30%. The setting is where the treatment can be switched on from zero. Write the setting paragraph as an argument about variation, and the reader stops treating the country as exotic.

The second move puts the reader’s own literature beside the result. Bar-Gill, Brynjolfsson, and Hak (2024) randomized eBay’s Seller Hub, a data-rich seller dashboard, and found that access raised sellers’ revenues by 3.6% on average. The same question in a rich platform setting produced an effect about a tenth the size. The outcomes, populations, and measurement all differ, so the comparison is a hypothesis about where analytics pays most, not an estimate. Stated that way, it gives a US reader a reason to care: your number is small because your firms already know what this treatment teaches.

The third move describes the firms by their economic role, not their geography. Most are retail shops, with some services such as hair salons (podcast). The registry frames them as the last mile through which large companies reach consumers in emerging markets. A brand manager at a consumer-goods firm recognizes that population at once.

The fourth move is a research program. The same team has varied the marketing lever while holding the population type fixed. Marketing versus finance training came first in South Africa (S. J. Anderson, Chandy, and Zia 2018), then volunteer marketers in Uganda (S. J. Anderson et al. 2021), customer-feedback seeking in Rwanda (Kaul et al. 2025), and now analytics. The Uganda paper appeared in the Journal of Marketing issue on better marketing for a better world, whose editorial invites work of this kind (Chandy et al. 2021). Each paper inherits the credibility of the last one’s fieldwork. A student with one emerging-market dataset should ask early which second paper the same population and instruments could support.

Two habits of style follow. Name the country in the setting section, not in the headline claim. And give the real reason for the choice of country alongside the scientific one. Chintagunta says plainly in the podcast that the study went to Rwanda partly because the research funding was there. Chintagunta also cites the country’s push on technology access and its heavy use of mobile payments. A paper can state both. It should not claim the country was picked for representativeness unless it was.

76.8.4 Evidence without hypothesis tests: the design is the argument

The specimen has no H1 through H4. In their place it has a design whose arms define the estimands, and outcome families reported in causal order. The table below reconstructs the estimands from the registry’s design.

Several practices then replace hypothesis-by-hypothesis testing.

  • Report outcome families in causal order. Usage, then mind, then practices, then money. Each family is reported as an effect with a confidence interval, not as a verdict on a hypothesis. The order is the story: a reader who has seen take-up and cognition is ready to believe the sales figure.
  • Separate the offer from the use. With usage low at first, the intent-to-treat effect answers the policy question of what offering the app does. Scaling by usage (treatment on the treated) answers how much using it does. Report both, and say which one the abstract quotes. The public versions do not say which estimate the 36.4% is.
  • Be exact about registration. The trial was registered on March 24, 2020, after the intervention began in July 2019, and no analysis plan appears on the public page. A writer in that position should say “registered” and not “pre-registered”, should name the primary outcomes (here sales and profits), and should label everything else as secondary or exploratory. Readers forgive late registration far more readily than a claim that turns out to be false.
  • Control multiplicity by family. Six cognitive tests and a list of practice items invite fishing. The standard remedy is a summary index per family, with p-values adjusted across families (M. L. Anderson 2008). That paper is in the specimen’s reference list, which suggests, though the public versions cannot confirm it, that the authors use this approach.
  • Show the mechanism through intermediate outcomes, and say what that cannot prove. The reference list includes the causal-mediation framework of Imai, Keele, and Tingley (2010). Cognition and practices were not themselves randomized, so a mediation estimate rests on sequential ignorability (Section 44.9.2). The safe claim is that the effect on intermediate outcomes and the effect on profits line up as the mechanism predicts. The placebo arm strengthens that claim, but it cannot turn it into an experiment on the mediator.
  • Treat heterogeneity as a test of mechanism, not a search. The reference list includes generalized random forests, debiased machine learning for conditional average treatment effects, and lasso-based selection of controls, the current toolkit for heterogeneity in experiments. Use the forest for discovery and label it that way. Separately, name two or three subgroups that the mechanism says should gain more, such as owners with weak baseline numeracy if the mechanism runs through calculation skill. In the podcast, Chintagunta says that the owners who already kept records showed directionally similar gains but were too few to test. Writing that sentence is the honest version of a heterogeneity result.
  • Benchmark the magnitude. A 29.2% profit gain means little until it is compared with something. The 2024 Booth Review article reports the authors’ cost calculation: about $4–$6 a month in variable cost, an unsubsidized up-front cost of $170–$210 per business, and break-even in roughly 7–10 months. Set that against the alternatives a funder would consider. The same team’s volunteer marketers raised monthly profits by 35.8% in Uganda (S. J. Anderson et al. 2021). Classroom training has a mixed record, which McKenzie (2021) reassesses. Intensive consulting worked for large Indian textile plants but at a much higher cost per firm (Bloom et al. 2013). Express the effect as a percentage of the control mean, in local currency and in dollars at a stated exchange rate, and per dollar spent.

76.8.5 The institutional section as persuasion

In a paper from an unfamiliar market, the setting and intervention sections do work that a literature review does elsewhere. They make the reader trust a design they cannot picture. Four kinds of detail carry most of the weight.

  • Who the firms are. Sector mix, size, how they were recruited, what “growth-oriented” meant as a screening rule, and how the sample compares with a national benchmark. The specimen’s reference list includes Rwanda’s 2020 Establishment Census, the natural benchmark for that comparison.
  • What the treatment was, screen by screen. What owners entered and how often, what came back, and what the visitors were and were not allowed to say. The podcast gives the level of detail a reader needs. Owners entered whether the shop was open and its revenue each day. Every two weeks they entered their top three products with price and cost, from which the app computed margins, together with counts of regular, occasional, and new customers. Detail of this kind is persuasive because it rules out the most damaging alternative, that the program was really free consulting. Visitors chosen for their lack of business experience serve the same purpose.
  • What everyone else received. Placebo firms had their data plans topped up, and every arm had enumerator visits (podcast). Balanced contact is the main answer to Hawthorne effects and experimenter demand, and it belongs in the design section, not in a footnote.
  • How the design changed. An earlier PEDL-funded project by the same team, active 2016–2018, describes a larger plan on its public page: 1,500 owners around Kigali, a finance-information tool and a marketing-information tool in separate arms, and follow-ups at 12 and 18–24 months. The public record does not say whether the executed study is a revision of that plan. A referee who finds such a page will ask. One paragraph explaining what changed and why pre-empts the question.

76.8.6 Would it work elsewhere?

The external-validity paragraph is where emerging-market papers most often say too much or too little. The productive form names the conditions under which the effect should travel, not a list of countries. For the specimen those conditions are plausibly three: owners do not already track their key numbers, the owner makes the decisions, and the phone and data cost little relative to monthly profit. Each condition can be checked against another market’s data. Chintagunta declines to extrapolate to US corner stores, saying such a claim would be “anecdotal” (podcast). That restraint is a model to copy. Two further caveats belong in the paragraph. The sample was screened for growth orientation, so the estimate describes firms that pass that screen, not the median microenterprise. And persistence is a separate question. The 2024 article reports a March 2021 follow-up of 14 randomly chosen treated owners, 13 of whom still kept records. Evidence that thin is useful as illustration and should be labeled as such, not counted as a long-run estimate.

76.8.7 Credible numbers where firms keep no books

The specimen’s measurement problem is general to the genre, and in one respect it is sharper. The published abstract says treated firms “report” higher sales and profits, and the verb matters: in settings without books, outcomes are self-reported. Here the treatment is record-keeping, so it changes the instrument that measures the outcome. Treated owners may report more accurately, or more optimistically, than control owners who are guessing. The defenses a referee will look for are these:

  1. Measure outcomes with the same enumerator protocol in every arm. Never use the app’s own records as the outcome for treated firms, because control firms have no such records.
  2. Collect several follow-up rounds and average them. Noisy outcomes like microenterprise profits gain more power from repeated measurement than from extra firms (McKenzie 2012), a paper the specimen cites.
  3. Cross-check reported profit against reported sales minus reported costs, and state the trimming or winsorizing rule before looking at treatment effects.
  4. Pair self-reports with outcomes that are hard to inflate. Business practices measured as a standard index of yes/no items (McKenzie and Woodruff 2017) and objective cognitive tests both qualify. In the podcast, Chintagunta describes the Cognitive Reflection Test (Frederick 2005), with about 0.7 of three items correct in the control group against about one in the treatment group. These are oral, approximate figures. The exact estimates are in the paper.
  5. Ask whether a test measures the trained skill or general ability. An owner who computes margins every two weeks has practiced arithmetic. A gain on a calculation test is near transfer. A gain on reasoning or memory tests is the more surprising claim and needs the stronger defense. The specimen’s reference list includes the cognitive-training literature in which this distinction is argued.
  6. Report attrition by arm and bound the estimates for it. The public versions give no attrition figures. The study ended as COVID-19 arrived, which makes the timing of the endline survey and the response rate worth a paragraph of their own.
  7. Account for local shocks. The reference list includes spatially robust standard errors and satellite night-lights data, which suggests the authors treat local economic conditions explicitly. That is worth doing whenever firms cluster in a few markets.

76.8.8 The anatomy of the genre

76.8.9 When your own data were not randomized

Most students with emerging-market data have a survey, a panel, or a partner’s transaction logs, not an experiment. Most of the template still applies. The country is still a source of variation, the institutional section still has to make a design believable, the outcome families can still be ordered as a chain, and the measurement defenses apply unchanged. What changes is the design paragraph. The arms that define the estimands become an identification argument: a policy rollout, a boundary, or a staggered adoption whose timing the firm did not choose. Those arguments are developed in Section 76.6.4 and Chapter 44. If no such argument is available, the honest genre is the descriptive paper (Section 76.3), whose contribution is a pattern that nobody had documented, stated with its own ceiling.

A checklist for writing your own emerging-market paper
  1. Write the setting paragraph as an argument about variation: say what the country lets you estimate that a rich-data market cannot.
  2. Put the closest result from a high-income setting beside yours, and explain the difference in magnitude as a hypothesis rather than a finding.
  3. Describe the firms by their economic role (retailers, suppliers, agents) and benchmark the sample against a national census or survey.
  4. State the contribution as an estimate, a measured mechanism, or a resolved tension, and name the decision maker who needs the number.
  5. Let the arms or the identifying variation define the estimands, and include a placebo or comparison that answers the most obvious objection.
  6. Report outcome families in causal order, one index per family, with multiplicity adjusted across families.
  7. Give both the effect of the offer and the effect of use, and say which one the abstract quotes.
  8. Say exactly when the study was registered and what was pre-specified.
  9. Present mechanisms through intermediate outcomes, and state the assumption that a mediation estimate needs.
  10. Name the subgroups the mechanism predicts before running exploratory heterogeneity, and report underpowered subgroups as underpowered.
  11. Measure outcomes with one protocol across arms, average several rounds, and pair self-reports with measures that are hard to inflate.
  12. Cost the intervention and compare it per dollar with the alternatives a funder would consider.
  13. Write the external-validity paragraph as a list of conditions, and label thin follow-up evidence as illustration.
  14. Give the real reason the study ran where it did, alongside the scientific one.

76.9 The Design-Science Method Paper

The methods paper sketched under paper types has a codified variant in information systems that marketing scholars increasingly write for, review for, and borrow from: the computational design-science paper. Its artifact is a method, usually a predictive model, and its contribution is design knowledge, meaning a statement of which design choices solve which problem and why (Hevner et al. 2004; Gregor and Hevner 2013; Abbasi et al. 2024). Students who know only the hypothesis-testing template find these papers hard to imitate, because the logic that holds them together is never stated in any one place. The paper reveals it through a handful of tables.

Two papers from the same September 2026 issue of Information Systems Research serve as specimens. Wang et al. (2026) propose DRDL, a deep-learning method that predicts whether and when a firm will fall into financial distress from several data sources at once (Section 56.3 reimplements it). Xu et al. (2026) propose UPSTAR, a product recommender that first infers why a customer bought each item, out of stable preference or exploratory intent, and then predicts the next purchase. The domains share almost nothing, but the architecture is the same, and the shared architecture is what to learn. (DRDL was read in full. For UPSTAR, only the published abstract and the authors’ released code were accessible when this section was written, so statements about UPSTAR’s internals come from the code.)

76.9.1 The spine: one artifact per challenge

The single most important object in a design-science paper is a table that most readers skim: the design framework. It runs from goals to challenges to design components, and it is built backward from the problem’s own features. DRDL’s version (their Table 2) has two goals, five challenges, and five components, one component for each challenge.

The table matters because every later section indexes into it. The method section has one subsection per row. The ablation study removes the rows one at a time. The comparison with related methods uses the challenges as its columns. The contribution section restates the goals as design principles. Two failure modes are visible at a glance. A component with no row is decoration, and a referee will ask why it is there. A challenge with no component is a promise the paper never redeems.

Each goal usually comes with a kernel theory, a theory from outside the method’s field that explains why the design should work. DRDL draws on the chunking theory of memory from cognitive psychology to justify discrete codes. UPSTAR starts from a framework of purchase motivations and keeps the two that are rooted in the consumer’s own interests. The kernel theory is inspiration, not a hypothesis under test, and the honest papers say so. DRDL calls it “a principled inspiration”. Referees judge it on whether the design traces back to it, not on whether the experiments confirm it.

76.9.2 The front half: question, gap table, rationale

The research questions are design questions, phrased as how to. DRDL’s two are how to separate useful from redundant information across data views, and how to predict risk over time while respecting two monotonicity constraints. The advice of Section 76.2.3 still applies, but differently: here the gap is a capability gap, so it has to be shown, not asserted. DRDL shows it with a positioning table of prior studies, with design properties as checkmark columns and “This study” as the last row. The table note states the search rule: studies from 2020–2025 in the AIS Senior Scholars’ list of premier journals and in the Academic Journal Guide’s operations research and management science category (rated 3 and above), 57 candidates in all. That note turns a literature review into an auditable claim. The table’s columns reuse the vocabulary of the design framework. So does a second table, which compares the proposed method with the incumbent methods on the same property columns.

Between the literature and the method sits a section that hypothesis-testing papers lack: methodological challenges and design rationale. It argues from the problem’s characteristics to each challenge, so that by the time the method appears, every component already has a reason to exist.

76.9.3 The method section

The method section follows a fixed order: a formal problem definition, an overview figure, one subsection per component, and a subsection explaining why the design should work (DRDL §4.7, “Mechanism of Disentanglement”). DRDL is also honest about novelty, a habit worth copying. Its contribution paragraph separates the existing building blocks it reuses, such as vector quantization and the multilayer perceptron, from the five it designed. A referee who finds an uncredited standard component discounts every other novelty claim in the paper.

76.9.4 Evaluation at three levels

Both papers evaluate at three levels, and DRDL names them: model, application, and mechanism.

Model: does it predict better? DRDL compares against 21 benchmarks from three method families. Sixteen of them are four multitask architectures, each combined with the monotonicity and ranking losses that earlier work proposed for the same two properties. The baselines thus get the best existing fix for each challenge rather than appearing as straw men. It runs five repetitions of 10-fold cross-validation for 50 estimates per cell, plus an out-of-time split. It reports ranking, horizon-specific, and calibration metrics. Two appendices pre-empt the predictable objections. Gradient boosting and parametric survival models on hand-built ratios answer “is the complexity worth it?” Averaging and stacking ensembles answer “isn’t this just an ensemble?” The headline is a C-index of 0.775 against 0.712 for the best benchmark on yearly Chinese-market prediction. UPSTAR’s abstract reports gains over state-of-the-art recommenders on three retail datasets.

Application: is the gain worth anything? Offline accuracy is not a decision, so the paper translates it into the currency of the person who acts on it (the same rule as item 8 above). DRDL simulates investment pools and counts the distressed firms each method lets in, scores profitability by return on assets and equity, and repeats the exercise under mean–variance weighting. For a recommender, the equivalent is what the recommendations do for the retailer. UPSTAR’s abstract stresses surfacing genuinely exploratory items, which drive discovery and cross-category sales.

Mechanism: why does it work? “Mechanism” here means something different from Stage 2 of Section 76.6, and it stands on firmer ground. The author controls the artifact, so removing a component is an intervention on the design rather than an inference from observational data. Five kinds of evidence recur:

  1. Ablation tied to the spine. Drop each component in turn. DRDL removes six, one at a time, and reports the performance gained per unit of training time for each. The mask-based fusion decoder delivers the most gain per second in both markets.
  2. Verify the property each component claims. If a component claims to disentangle, measure disentanglement directly. DRDL scores its representations on two disentanglement metrics against two disentangled-VAE baselines. A component whose claimed property is never measured has only an ablation to its name, and an ablation cannot say why the drop happened.
  3. Locate the gain where the theory predicts it. UPSTAR’s headline mechanism evidence is that the improvement concentrates on exploration-driven purchases. That is where a motivation-aware design should help and a motivation-blind one should struggle.
  4. Rule out the cheap explanations: more parameters, ensembling, class imbalance.
  5. Sensitivity and interpretability: vary the hyperparameters the design introduced (codebook size in DRDL, the stable and exploratory cutoffs in UPSTAR), and show what the learned representations encode.

DRDL runs seven such analyses, most of them in online appendices. The main text carries the ablation and the property check, because those two tie the evidence back to the spine.

76.9.5 Make the elaborate version beat the simple one

UPSTAR’s released code shows why the simple version of your own idea should appear in the paper. In the code, the paper’s STB measure works like this. It builds an item co-purchase graph and perturbs it adversarially. It then scores each item by how little its learned embedding moves: robust items count as stable preference, fragile ones as exploratory. Within each customer’s history, the top half of items by score are labelled stable and the bottom 40% exploratory. The repository’s configuration offers three STB variants. Its help text describes a repurchase-intensity score as “default & best” and the original adversarial version as “degenerate”. The repository ships training code but no evaluation script. None of this shows that the published results are wrong, and we have not rerun them. It does show the question a replicator will ask first: does the sophisticated component earn its place over a one-line heuristic for the same construct? The defense is to put that heuristic in the paper as a baseline and beat it. The second defense is to release the code that regenerates the headline table, not only the training loop.

76.9.6 Carrying the template into a marketing journal

Design-science outlets judge the artifact. Marketing journals reading the same paper weigh three further things.

  • Validity of any new measure. A score like STB is a measurement claim: that a number computed from transaction logs tracks a psychological motivation. The standards of Section 39.4 apply. That means convergent evidence against an external criterion, such as stated motivation or a known exploration episode, and discriminant evidence against confounds such as purchase frequency.
  • Decision value shown in the field. An offline accuracy table persuades an IS referee more than a marketing one. A field experiment, or a credible policy counterfactual, carries the application level further.
  • The marketing question in front. UPSTAR’s motivation framework is the marketing hook. The architecture is the means. A marketing version of the paper leads with what the framework says about consumers and treats the recommender as the test of that framework.
A checklist for the design-science method paper
  1. Phrase each research question as how to design something that achieves a stated property.
  2. Build the design framework (Table 76.12) before drafting. Every component gets exactly one challenge, and every challenge gets a component.
  3. Name the kernel theory, and present it as inspiration for the design, not a hypothesis the experiments test.
  4. Back the gap claim with a positioning table whose selection rule sits in the table note, and reuse its property columns to compare against incumbent methods.
  5. Separate reused building blocks from novel ones in the contribution statement.
  6. Benchmark across method families, give strong baselines the best existing fix for each challenge, and report variance across repeated splits plus an out-of-time test.
  7. Include the simple heuristic version of your own idea, and a tuned off-the-shelf learner on hand-built features, as baselines.
  8. Translate accuracy into a decision outcome measured in the user’s currency.
  9. Ablate one component at a time, measure the property each component claims, and show the gain landing where the kernel theory predicts.
  10. State the contribution as design principles, and release code that reproduces the headline table, not only the training loop.

76.10 The Structural-Model Paper: A Consumer-Search Specimen

A third paper from the same September 2026 issue of Information Systems Research shows a different genre, the empirical structural-model paper. Zhang et al. (2026) model how consumers search across a platform’s native app and its mini-program, carrying a reference price from one channel to the other, and use the estimates to design a promotion (Section 53.5.3 covers the substance). The artifact here is not a method to be benchmarked, as in Section 76.9, nor a causal effect, as in Section 76.6. It is an estimated model of behavior, and the contribution is what the model lets a decision maker do that a reduced-form analysis cannot. Structural papers in marketing, economics, and IS share a skeleton, and this one shows it clearly. (Only the two versions of the abstract and the deposited reference list were accessible when this section was written, so what follows reads the paper’s framing, not its internals.)

76.10.1 The title and the abstract

The title has two halves joined by a colon, a phenomenon and a model: “Analyzing Consumer Footprints on E-Commerce Platforms: A Multichannel Sequential Search Model with Reference Price.” The first half echoes Ghose, Ipeirotis, and Li (2019), “Modeling Consumer Footprints on Search Engines,” and that echo positions the paper in an IS tradition before the reader reaches the abstract. The second half lists the model’s ingredients in order of novelty: multichannel is new, sequential search is the inherited framework, and reference price is the behavioral addition.

The Crossref abstract makes six moves in seven sentences, and each is one or two sentences long:

  1. Context. Mini-programs let consumers browse across the app and the mini-program, leaving click and purchase records in both.
  2. Opportunity. These multichannel footprints contain information about search preferences that could improve multichannel management.
  3. Gap. Prior studies focus on single-channel contexts that “may not directly apply.”
  4. Model. A threefold search across channels, products, and pages, with a reference price updated along the journey.
  5. Findings. Heterogeneity in channel preferences, cross-channel costs, and reference-price sensitivity explains the variety of footprints.
  6. Policy. A 32% average promotion gap between channels, and more profit from a smaller promotion than the state-of-the-art model achieves.

A second abstract, on the paper’s record in City University of Hong Kong’s repository and marked “© 2026, INFORMS”, swaps move 5 for a prediction claim (“significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art sequential search models in predicting both clicks and purchases”) and quantifies move 6 as a 22% profit improvement. That pairing is the genre’s signature: the model is first shown to be right (it predicts held-out behavior better than the incumbent model) and then shown to be useful (it changes a decision, by an amount in money).

76.10.2 The spine: data feature, model component, counterfactual lever

The design-science paper is held together by a table of challenges and components (Table 76.12). The structural paper’s equivalent links three things: a feature of the data that the incumbent model cannot reproduce, the model component added to reproduce it, and the counterfactual lever that the component makes available. A component that changes no counterfactual is hard to justify; a lever with no component behind it is a promise the paper cannot keep.

The table also says where to spend pages. The paper has to show model-free evidence for every data feature in the first column before the model appears (for example, that consumers who saw a lower price in one channel click differently in the other), because a referee who does not believe the feature will not believe the component.

76.10.3 The sections, and what each must contain

A structural search paper usually runs in this order.

  1. Introduction, ending with the policy number and a contribution paragraph for each literature the paper joins. This paper joins three, as its reference list shows: consumer search (Weitzman-type models from Weitzman (1979) to Morozov et al. (2021)), reference prices (Mazumdar, Raj, and Sinha (2005); Putler (1992)), and multichannel and mobile commerce. The contribution claim works because the three have rarely been combined. That is the “intersection” gap of Section 76.2, and it holds only if the intersection is really empty, which leads to the next item.
  2. Literature, organized by stream, closing each stream with what this paper adds. The closest prior work deserves a paragraph of its own. The nearest predecessor here is Hu and Karacaoglu (2024), a Production and Operations Management paper on the same app versus mini-program comparison, estimated on JD.com data with a sequential search model. It does not appear in the ISR paper’s deposited reference list. Whether the two were developed in parallel we cannot tell. The lesson for authors is general: search the adjacent fields (operations, IS, economics) for the closest competitor, because a referee from that field will know it.
  3. Data and model-free evidence. Sessions, channels, click order, prices, and purchases, with descriptive patterns tied to the spine’s first column.
  4. Model. Utility, search costs, the reference-price process, and the decision rules, stated as equations, with every departure from the canonical model flagged. A reference price that updates with prices seen during the search breaks one of Weitzman’s independence assumptions. An honest paper says what the consumer is assumed to anticipate and what she is not.
  5. Identification. Which variation in the data pins down which parameter: click order for preferences, stopping for search costs, cross-channel price differences for the reference-price parameters. The framework of Ursu, Seiler, and Honka (2025) is now the standard reference for this argument.
  6. Estimation: the simulator, its tuning, and a Monte Carlo study showing that the estimator recovers known parameters (Section 53.5.4 does this for a stylized version).
  7. Results: parameter estimates, heterogeneity, and fit against benchmark search models and machine-learning predictors (this paper’s reference list includes a deep click-prediction model, xDeepFM).
  8. Counterfactuals. The policy simulation, compared against the policy the benchmark model would have recommended. Choose counterfactuals the normalizations permit: price and promotion changes rather than search-cost changes.
  9. Robustness and conclusion.
A checklist for the structural search paper
  1. Make the title name the phenomenon first and the model second.
  2. Build the spine (Table 76.13) before drafting: every new component answers a data feature and opens a counterfactual lever.
  3. Show model-free evidence for each data feature before the model.
  4. Flag every departure from the canonical model, and say what it costs in optimality or identification.
  5. Argue identification parameter by parameter, from the variation in the data.
  6. Run a Monte Carlo recovery study for the estimator and report the tuning choices.
  7. Beat the incumbent structural model and a flexible predictive model out of sample.
  8. Run counterfactuals the normalizations allow, and compare against the incumbent model’s recommendation.
  9. Search adjacent fields for the closest prior paper and position against it explicitly.

76.11 The Observational Contagion Paper: A Fraud-Spread Specimen

Many marketing and finance questions are about spread: of word of mouth, of a product, of a misconduct norm, of an investing habit. Usually there is no experiment and no clean shock, only outcomes by place or person and a measured network. Papers in this genre cannot claim identification in the strict sense, so their persuasiveness depends on structure. Griffin, Kruger, and Mahajan (2026), on fraud in the U.S. Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), is a well-built recent example from The Review of Financial Studies. The econometrics, with our replication from the authors’ package, are in Section 52.5.1. This section reads the paper as a piece of writing.

76.11.1 Title and abstract

The title is a yes-or-no question with a subtitle naming the setting: “Is Fraud Contagious? Social Connections and the Looting of COVID Relief Programs.” The question repeats the title of Dimmock, Gerken, and Graham (2018), who asked it about coworkers at financial-advisory firms. Reusing a known question tells finance readers which literature the paper extends before they read a word of the abstract. The subtitle supplies the channel (social connections) and a vivid object (“looting”).

The abstract makes four moves in four sentences. It states a fact: fraud is geographically concentrated. It states the main finding: high-fraud places are socially linked, and fraud spreads over time along those links. It gives mechanism evidence: members of fraud-promoting social media groups commit more fraud, and linked places use the same FinTech lenders. It closes with policy: faster, data-driven detection and prosecution. The abstract has no identification jargon. The identification argument starts in the introduction.

76.11.2 Rival hypotheses before the favored one

Section 1.2 sets out three hypotheses before any result. The first is an individualist null: some people were more willing to commit fraud and took the chance. If so, local crime, culture and demographics should explain where fraud happened, and social ties should add nothing. The second is organized cybercrime using stolen identities, which predicts a link to past identity theft. The third, social transmission, is grounded in Sutherland’s differential-association theory of crime: people learn both the techniques and the rationalizations for an offense from their contacts.

The paper then gives the first two hypotheses a real test. Section 2 regresses fraud on demographics, religious affiliation, public corruption, identity theft, suspicious-activity reports and social capital, and it reports what works (identity theft, poverty, race) as partial support for both. Only then does the social measure arrive, and it wins on incremental \(R^2\): it explains about ten times as much within-county variation as the strongest demographic variable. Giving the favored hypothesis a fair fight against named rivals is more persuasive than testing it alone. It also answers in advance the referee who asks “isn’t this just poverty?”

76.11.3 The spine: one section per referee question

After the main estimate, every subsection heading in Section 3 is a question a skeptical reader would ask, and each is answered by one exhibit.

Building this table before drafting is the most useful thing to take from the specimen. List the worries a referee will raise, give each one a heading and an exhibit, and order them from the most obvious alternative to the most subtle. Section 3.5 is the section referees read most closely. The paper names the threat by its canonical source, Manski’s reflection problem (Manski 1993). It concedes that the threat is hard to eliminate. It then lists five numbered responses, each pointing back to evidence already shown. Conceding the limit first makes the numbered responses easier to trust.

76.11.4 Moves worth copying

  • Description first. Figure 1 shows a county map, then within-county variation across ZIP codes, then fraud rates over time by lender type. The reader sees the variation to be explained before any model tries to explain it.
  • A network figure that makes an argument. Figure 2 places ZIP codes of three cities on the sides of a triangle, sorted by fraud decile, with edge width showing tie strength. High-fraud nodes visibly connect to each other. Most network plots show only that a network exists. This one shows the result.
  • Magnitude in a portable unit. All variables are standardized, so every coefficient reads in standard deviations, and the incremental-\(R^2\) comparison gives a sentence readers remember (“ten times the next predictor”).
  • Fingerprint outcomes as mechanism evidence.
