The strongest section concerns outcomes that homophily cannot easily produce: clusters of loans identical in industry, amount and headcount, and the choice of a particular FinTech platform. A refrain recurs at the end of each mechanism test, that the pattern would be “difficult to explain if social connections merely proxy for homophily.” Repeating one sentence ties the separate tests to a single claim.
  • Qualitative texture. Group names and posts from fraud-promoting social media groups (“sauce”, “methods”), and word clouds contrasting high- and low-fraud groups, make the mechanism concrete. The full posts go in an appendix exhibit. Differential-association theory explains why both techniques and rationalizations show up in them.
  • Robustness in footnotes. The body states each robustness result in one sentence and points to the Internet Appendix, which has about twenty tables. Weighting and clustering are stated once in a footnote and then kept the same throughout.
  • Calibrated language. The heterogeneity results “may alleviate (though not eliminate)” concerns about omitted variables. Hedges like that one show readers the authors know where the evidence stops.
  • Policy that follows from the finding. The policy point concerns speed: fraud spreading through networks outran the program’s pay-now, chase-later model. That conclusion depends on the spread result, so it does not read as an afterthought.

76.11.5 Where the specimen is thin

A referee reading the paper with Section 52.5.1 open would press on three points. First, linked places can be targeted together, for example by social media advertising. That is a common shock that travels along ties, and none of the tests separates it from person-to-person transmission. Second, the network is measured in 2021, after the program began, so the design assumes ties predate the fraud. Third, the Oster bound depends on the assumed maximum \(R^2\) (Section 44.10), and the paper uses one value. None of these sinks the paper, but a manuscript of this genre should raise each point itself, in Section 3.5’s list, before the referee does.

76.11.6 Carrying the template into a marketing journal

The same skeleton fits a word-of-mouth or adoption paper using place-level outcomes and the public county-to-county Social Connectedness Index (Bailey, Cao, Kuchler, Stroebel, and Wong 2018). The contribution paragraph should name which of four evidence types the paper supplies, because marketing referees will rank them. A shock to the network itself, as in Dimmock, Gerken, and Graham (2018)’s use of firm mergers, ranks highest. Next comes a shock to one’s contacts that does not touch oneself, as in Bailey, Cao, Kuchler, and Stroebel (2018). A fingerprint outcome ranks third, as in Maturana and Nickerson (2019)’s same-lender choices among teachers. A stacked falsification battery alone comes last. The specimen combines the third and fourth. Say plainly which ones you have, and title the effect accordingly: “social transmission is consistent with” is a defensible claim from a battery, “the causal peer effect is” is not.

A checklist for the observational contagion paper
  1. Ask the question in the title; if a well-known paper asked it in another setting, echo that title.
  2. State rival hypotheses before the favored one, with the prediction each makes, and give the rivals a real test.
  3. Show the raw variation (maps, within-unit spread, time paths) before any regression.
  4. Define the exposure measure as an equation, and exclude the nearest units (own county, own firm) so it cannot be mechanical.
  5. Report magnitude in a portable unit: standardized coefficients plus incremental \(R^2\).
  6. Build the spine (Table 76.14): one heading per referee worry, one exhibit per heading.
  7. Name the reflection problem explicitly, concede what cannot be ruled out, then list your responses.
  8. Find at least one fingerprint outcome that only shared information could produce.
  9. Add qualitative evidence of what was transmitted, with the raw material in an appendix.
  10. State weighting, clustering and standardization once, and keep them fixed across tables. Standardized coefficients change with the standardization sample.
  11. Rank your evidence type against shock-based designs and phrase the causal claim to match.

76.12 The Theory-Building Paper: Naming a Construct from Hidden Data

Some papers earn their place by changing how a field looks at a phenomenon. They name a construct nobody had named, show how to observe it, sort its variants, and end with what institutions should do about it. This is the inductive theory-building paper. It is the house genre of Organization Science, Administrative Science Quarterly, and the Academy of Management Journal, and marketing journals publish it too, in consumer culture theory and in conceptual-empirical work. It is hard to learn from the hypothesis-testing template, because the contribution is not an estimate. It is a concept, a classification of the concept’s forms, and an argument about where a boundary lies.

Weiss and Radoynovska (2026a) is a clean specimen. The authors ask how entrepreneurs carry out criminal deception, meaning the use of deceptive means to defraud audiences. They answer from the court records of 12 Silicon Valley technology ventures whose founders were prosecuted for securities, wire, or bank fraud between 2000 and 2023. The answer is a new construct, façading. Entrepreneurs construct, perform, and protect an illusory appearance of a high-growth venture that masks the venture’s actual underperformance, and they do it in three forms keyed to how far the venture has fallen behind what its audiences expect. The paper closes with remedies addressed to the SEC, to investors, and to entrepreneurship educators. (This section was written from the authors’ accepted manuscript (Weiss and Radoynovska 2026b). Section and table numbers follow that version and may differ slightly in print.)

76.12.1 The spine: one construct, three sub-processes, three forms

The paper makes ten moves, and each one transfers to other topics.

76.12.2 Seeing something new

The paper’s new way of looking rests on three reframings, and none of them needs new vocabulary.

  1. From discourse to the discourse–organizing interface. Earlier work studied the stories entrepreneurs tell. This paper studies the organizing that lets a false story survive checking: the doctored invoices, forged term sheets, staged demos, and impersonated reference calls.
  2. From the future to the past. The earlier literature treats deception as part of future-making, in the form of aspirational claims about what a venture will do. The prosecuted founders fabricated what the venture had already done: booked revenue, recurring customers, a completed audit. The authors argue that fictionalizing the past is the hallmark of the criminal form.
  3. From the entrepreneur to the institution. Silicon Valley’s unicorn ideal sets what audiences expect at each stage, so the gap founders backfill is set by the ecosystem, not only by their own pitches.

Each reframing is a contrast a referee can check against the literature cited, and that is what makes it defensible. A lens the referee cannot check against prior work reads as a label.

Positioning against the nearest neighbor takes one clause. The paper cites a 2022 working paper by Mohliver, Karp, and Zuzul titled Dominant Deceptions, which appears to be an earlier version of Zuzul and Mohliver (2026). That project follows a single venture and traces how deception spreads inside it. Weiss and Radoynovska (2026a) describe that work as being about how deception diffuses within ventures, and they claim a different question: how deception is carried out, compared across ventures. Both papers build on an expectation–reality gap, and their answers fit together. One traces the drift from “we will” to “we have” inside one firm. The other sorts the finished schemes across firms. When a close competitor exists, name it, say which question it answers, and claim a different one.

76.12.3 Defining the construct

The definition is built in three steps. It starts from a noun the field already uses. In the organizational definition the authors adopt, a façade is a symbolic front that reassures stakeholders of the organization’s legitimacy. The noun then becomes a process, façading. Finally, the process is split into sub-processes a coder can find in a document:

  • constructing the façade, through fictionalized stories, fabricated evidence, staged product demos, co-opted verification, and manipulated regulatory compliance;
  • performing it before the audiences that hold resources;
  • protecting it from scrutiny.

A construct also needs a boundary, because a construct defined only by its center gets stretched to fit everything (Chapter 3). The paper draws the line between ordinary entrepreneurial dramatization and criminal deception. Entrepreneurs cross it when their stories become detached from the venture’s operational reality and are propped up by organized fabrication of evidence. That boundary is what makes the construct useful, because it tells an educator, an investor, or a juror which side of the line a given act falls on.

The typology is cumulative. Surface façading fictionalizes stories of imminent success. Reinforced façading adds interlocking sets of faked historical evidence and central control of information. Deep façading adds faked product demos, co-opted due diligence, manipulated regulatory compliance, and organized secrecy. Each form contains the acts of the one before it (their Table 3). That makes the scheme easy to apply and hard to dispute at the margins. The authors also report what they did not see. They call the process discontinuous because no venture in the data moved from one form to the next, and they say such a progression is possible but unobserved.

76.12.4 Measuring it: data that make the hidden visible

Criminal deception is hidden by design, which is why earlier research theorized it mostly through its causes and consequences. The paper’s main methodological move is to find data in which the hidden part is already documented. Court records are produced adversarially. Prosecutors must prove each deceptive act with exhibits, and defendants contest the evidence. The sample is defined as a filter a reader could rerun:

  • federal securities-fraud charges and the related wire, bank, and conspiracy statutes;
  • the Northern District of California;
  • cases between 2000 and 2023;
  • privately held, equity-financed, high-growth technology ventures;
  • fraud within ten years of founding.

The filter excludes public companies, fraud tied to an IPO, and SEC investigations that settled or closed without a public record. A second search then collects every further case against the same founders.

The analysis section is unusually long, and the authors say why: inductive analysis of court records is rare in organization science. It has five steps:

  1. selecting documents (complaints, indictments, plea agreements, sentencing memoranda, and trial transcripts, but not procedural filings);
  2. in vivo coding of the first three ventures;
  3. building a codebook by moving between the data and the literature;
  4. drawing a timeline for each venture, with its funding rounds overlaid;
  5. comparing the twelve cases.

Two choices are worth copying. In the last step, the authors built tables to test rival explanations before settling on the life-cycle gap. They checked whether sophistication depended on how early the deception began, and on how long it lasted. They also pseudonymized every venture although the records are public, because the aim is patterns across cases, not singling out deviant individuals.

The headline numbers in the introduction can be checked against the paper’s own Table 1. Run this check on your own manuscript before you submit it.

Code
# The 12 ventures of Weiss & Radoynovska (2026), from their Tables 1 and 3.
# capital_musd: equity capital raised, $ million. prison_months: summed over all
# defendants (founders, co-founders, executives); 0 = civil case only; NA = pending.
cases <- data.frame(
  venture = c("Speedify", "TakeOff", "RapidLauncher",
              "QuickSnap", "ProfitDash", "Accelify", "RevenueBoost",
              "ScaleX", "Tracton", "UnicornHealth", "HyperJet", "GrowthHacker"),
  form = factor(rep(c("Surface", "Reinforced", "Deep"), c(3, 4, 5)),
                levels = c("Surface", "Reinforced", "Deep")),
  capital_musd  = c(12, 22, 1.13, 115.7, 4.5, 204.5, 7.3,
                    910.41, 17.6, 104.79, 93.77, 0.30),
  court_cases   = c(1, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1, 1, 6, 2, 3, 5, 2),   # appeals counted as cases
  prison_months = c(0, 24, 8, 18, 36, 0, 88, 135 + 155, 30, NA, 180 + 160, 36),
  pages         = c(28, 64, 53, 153, 58, 25, 94, 2702, 68, 135, 521, 121)
)

# Audit the introduction's headline totals against the table.
data.frame(
  quantity   = c("Ventures", "Court cases", "Prison sentences (years)",
                 "Equity capital raised ($ million)"),
  stated     = c(12, 27, 73, 1800),
  from_table = c(nrow(cases), sum(cases$court_cases),
                 sum(cases$prison_months, na.rm = TRUE) / 12,
                 sum(cases$capital_musd))
)
#>                            quantity stated from_table
#> 1                          Ventures     12       12.0
#> 2                       Court cases     27       27.0
#> 3          Prison sentences (years)     73       72.5
#> 4 Equity capital raised ($ million)   1800     1494.0

# How much of the coded evidence each form of facading rests on.
by_form <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cases, cases$form), function(d) data.frame(
  form           = as.character(d$form[1]),
  ventures       = nrow(d),
  median_capital = median(d$capital_musd),
  court_pages    = sum(d$pages),
  share_of_pages = round(sum(d$pages) / sum(cases$pages), 2)
)))
rownames(by_form) <- NULL
by_form
#>         form ventures median_capital court_pages share_of_pages
#> 1    Surface        3          12.00         145           0.04
#> 2 Reinforced        4          61.50         330           0.08
#> 3       Deep        5          93.77        3547           0.88

Three of the four totals reproduce: 12 ventures, 27 court cases (counting appeals as cases), and 72.5 prison-years, which the introduction rounds to 73. The capital raised does not. The per-venture figures sum to $1.49 billion against $1.8 billion in the text, and we could not reconcile the two. The published version may have corrected one or the other. The $687.6 million in losses cannot be rebuilt from the table at all. Table 1 mixes restitution, disgorgement, and forfeiture, and two co-founders owe the same $93 million in restitution. The rule for your own paper is that every number in the introduction should be recomputable from a table in the paper, with the aggregation rule stated in the table note.

The page counts carry a second lesson. Deep-façading cases supply 88% of the 4,022 coded pages, and ScaleX, the one venture whose founder went to a jury trial, supplies 2,702 pages by itself. The most sophisticated form is therefore observed through the deepest records, and records are deepest where a defendant fought the charges. A referee could fairly ask whether part of what separates the forms is documentation rather than behavior, since a guilty plea leaves a thin file. The rival explanations the authors report concern timing and duration, not record depth. If your data source’s coverage varies with your construct, say so, and show that the construct holds among cases with comparable records.

The gap itself can be measured with numbers, which points to a quantitative follow-up. Where a complaint quotes a claimed figure beside the true one, their ratio measures how far the façade had drifted from reality.

Code
# Claimed versus actual figures quoted from the complaints in the findings section.
gap <- data.frame(
  venture = c("QuickSnap", "Accelify", "HyperJet"),
  form    = c("Reinforced", "Reinforced", "Deep"),
  metric  = c("Revenue, Q1 2018 ($)", "Gross revenue, 2013 ($ million)",
              "Client accounts, mid-2009"),
  claimed = c(6043369, 101, 1012002),
  actual  = c(1300381, 9.5, 81618)
)
gap$inflation <- round(gap$claimed / gap$actual, 1)
gap
#>     venture       form                          metric claimed    actual
#> 1 QuickSnap Reinforced            Revenue, Q1 2018 ($) 6043369 1300381.0
#> 2  Accelify Reinforced Gross revenue, 2013 ($ million)     101       9.5
#> 3  HyperJet       Deep       Client accounts, mid-2009 1012002   81618.0
#>   inflation
#> 1       4.6
#> 2      10.6
#> 3      12.4

Three ventures, each measured at a different stage and on a different metric, do not make a test. Collected across hundreds of SEC complaints, a ratio like this would let the paper’s central proposition be tested: that deception becomes more elaborate as the gap widens.

76.12.5 Findings as a grid

Each findings subsection has the same internal order:

  1. an opening paragraph that places the form in the life cycle and states the size of the gap;
  2. three parts, on constructing, performing, and protecting the façade, each headed by a run-in sentence that states the finding (for example, “Protecting the façade through passing blame”);
  3. a closing paragraph that restates the form in one sentence and leads into the next form.

Each subsection draws on three to five ventures. The evidence is block quotations from complaints, sentencing memoranda, and plea agreements. Evidence that would only repeat what the previous form already showed goes to an online appendix (footnotes 6 and 9 say so), and the main text shows only what is new at each level. A reader can turn to any cell of the three-by-three grid and find the same structure.

76.12.6 Drawing the theory

The paper’s Figure 1 puts the theory in one picture. The venture life cycle runs along the horizontal axis and performance up the vertical one. A steep curve, topped with a unicorn icon, marks the performance audiences expect. A lower curve, ending in a horse icon, marks actual performance. The area between them is shaded and widens from left to right, and the three forms of façading label three regions of it. Breaks in the expectation curve encode the claim that ventures enter a form directly rather than passing through all three. Figure 76.10 lays out the argument the figure compresses.

76.12.7 Contributions: arguments first, then literatures

The discussion opens with a subsection titled “Toward a Theory of Criminal Deception”. It states four numbered arguments before it mentions any literature:

  1. Façading backfills the gap between expected and actual performance.
  2. The form of façading depends on the size of the gap.
  3. The theory sits at the discourse–organizing interface.
  4. The venture’s projected appearance becomes progressively detached from its reality.

The fourth argument climbs a ladder of metaphors: a veneer laid over the real venture, then a standalone artifact that audiences deal with instead of the venture, then a staged parallel world like the one in The Truman Show. Each metaphor names a different level of detachment, so the ladder adds content rather than decoration.

Only then come the contributions, one subsection for each of three literatures (cultural entrepreneurship, organizational wrongdoing, and the social effects of entrepreneurship), and each ends with a research agenda. One claim is built to be quoted and argued with: verifiability, not authenticity, is the right guard against deception, because authenticity judgments reward the rule-breaking and hubris that entrepreneurial culture already prizes. A contrarian claim that can be tested is often the sentence later papers cite.

76.12.8 Proposing a solution

The practical implications say who should act and how. Lower the barriers to whistleblowing, and extend SEC whistleblower protection to startup employees. Introduce SEC audits of ventures late in the life cycle. Hold investors who sit on boards more accountable, and have them check claims against several independent sources during due diligence. Teach entrepreneurship students where permissible dramatization ends and criminal façading begins. The remedies also enter a live debate in legal scholarship over whether the SEC should police private markets, which gives the paper readers beyond its own field.

The remedies persuade because they follow from the findings. Table 76.16 sets each protection approach beside what defeated it in the cases and the remedy that would make that outcome more likely. We compiled the middle column from the findings section; the paper does not tabulate how each façade was unmasked.

Insiders unmasked five of the eight façades whose unmasking the findings describe: an intern, an employee, a new CFO, employees who went to regulators and the press, and a general counsel. That pattern is the empirical case for putting whistleblowers first, and a reader can see it in the evidence without being told. The paper does not test any remedy, which is acceptable in Organization Science, where practical implications follow from the theory. Marketing’s policy outlets set a higher bar (Chapter 75). There a remedy should be evaluated, or at least costed, before it is recommended.

76.12.9 Carrying the template into a marketing journal

Marketing has its own archives in which hidden behavior was forced into the open. FTC complaints and consent orders, National Advertising Division decisions, state attorney-general actions, and class-action filings all document deceptive claims with exhibits, as these court records do. The construct travels too. One deep-façading venture sold “AI” insights that were partly produced by paid human workers watching videos, the pattern now called AI washing. Greenwashing, fake reviews, and vaporware announcements (Chapter 29) are other cases in which a claim and the organizing behind it can come apart. Three adjustments help a marketing version get through review.

  • Put the market stake in front. A marketing referee will ask what the construct changes for buyers, competitors, or regulators, not only for theory.
  • Pair the typology with a measure that scales. The coding rules in Table 76.15 (facets deceived, audience, protection approach) can become labels for a text classifier run over thousands of enforcement documents (Chapter 47). A claimed-to-actual ratio like the one above is a continuous measure of the gap. The typology then becomes a hypothesis the next study can test at scale.
  • State the boundary as a decision rule. The line between dramatization and criminal deception has a counterpart in advertising law, the line between puffery and a material misrepresentation. A paper that tells readers which side of it a claim falls on is useful to managers and regulators alike.
A checklist for the theory-building paper
  1. Place the phenomenon on a continuum the field already studies, and name the segment nobody has studied.
  2. Open with one or two named public cases before the anonymized data.
  3. Show that each relevant literature holds half of the phenomenon, and borrow the lens from an existing distinction.
  4. Find data in which the hidden behavior is already documented, and write the sample as a filter someone could rerun.
  5. Build the construct from a definition readers accept, split it into sub-processes a coder can find, and state the boundary where it stops applying.
  6. Make the typology cumulative if you can, and say which transitions you did not observe.
  7. Report the rival explanations you checked, and check whether the depth of your data varies with the construct.
  8. Give every cell of the typology the same structure in the findings, and move repeated evidence to an appendix.
  9. Draw the construct as a quantity in one figure.
  10. State the theoretical arguments before the contributions to each literature, and end each contribution with a research agenda.
  11. Derive each remedy from a finding, address it to a named institution, and say whether it was tested.
  12. Make every headline number recomputable from a table in the paper.

76.13 The Measurement Paper: A New Variable from Text

A measurement paper names something that matters and that no dataset records, builds a variable for it from a source nobody had mined for that purpose, and then spends most of its pages showing that the variable behaves the way the thing itself should. The contribution is the variable. The regressions are there to earn the reader’s trust in it, and none of them needs to identify a causal effect. Finance and accounting publish this genre steadily, with text-based measures of competition, financial constraints, corporate culture, and brand value among the well-known cases (Li et al. 2021; Boustanifar and Kang 2025), and it is the most direct route by which unstructured data (Chapter 47) becomes a top-journal paper.

Boustanifar and Verriest (2026) is a specimen worth taking apart because the method is as simple as the genre allows. The measure is a word count. Whatever persuades the reader therefore comes from the architecture of the paper, and that architecture can be copied. The authors start from an accounting rule. A liability goes on the balance sheet only if it is probable and can be reliably estimated. Anything else, such as a pending lawsuit, a product-liability exposure, an environmental obligation, or a false-advertising or patent-infringement claim, is disclosed in the text of the annual report and nowhere in the numbers. They call these obligations intangible liabilities (IL), count the words that signal them in every 10-K filed between fiscal years 1996 and 2020, and show that the count predicts lawsuits, reputational damage, valuation, stock returns, and crash risk. (This section was written from the authors’ accepted manuscript (Boustanifar and Verriest 2023), in its April 2026 revision marked as forthcoming in Management Science. Table numbers and estimates follow that version and may differ slightly in print.)

76.13.1 The spine: define, build, validate, price

The abstract follows the same order at one sentence per step: the accounting rule, examples, the name, the measure, its correlates, what it predicts, how it is priced, and the implication. A reader who stops after the abstract already knows what the construct is and why it has stakes. That matters more in this genre than in most, because there is no clever identification strategy to carry the reader’s interest.

76.13.2 Defining the construct before measuring it

The definition is borrowed from a rule, which makes the boundary of the construct checkable. An intangible liability is an economically significant obligation that fails the recognition test (probable and estimable) and so appears only in text. A footnote then separates it from the neighboring accounting category. Disclosed contingent liabilities are a subset, because a firm can be exposed to a kind of harm, such as personal injury from its products, before any claim exists, and that exposure is written up under risk factors. The footnote is also the argument for measuring over the whole filing. A measure built only on the legal-proceedings section would capture the subset and miss the construct.

A second footnote settles what “intangible” means. It is not “cannot be touched.” It is “cannot be appraised at an actual or approximate value.” Human capital can be touched and is off the balance sheet. A firm’s cryptocurrency cannot be touched and is on it. Two sentences of this kind close off the most likely misreading of a new label, and a new construct should always get them (Chapter 3).

The positioning against prior work is equally short. Accounting research already measures litigation risk, the probability of being sued (I. Kim and Skinner 2012). The authors grant that it is one source of intangible liabilities and list others that it leaves out: pending suits, recalls, guarantees, environmental obligations, and pending legislation. They later add litigation-risk measures as controls. The claim is that the new construct is broader than its nearest neighbor, and the paper supports the claim with a definition in the front and a regression in the back.

76.13.3 Building the measure, and the three decisions inside a word count

A dictionary measure looks like it involves no decisions. This one involves three, and the paper defends each.

Which words. The starting list was built to measure tone, so many of its entries are legalistic words with no bearing on obligations (hereby, shall, aforementioned). The authors read how each word is used in filings before deciding. Interrogate appears in biotech filings about interrogating cells. Designator is an airline code. Extracorporeal is a medical procedure. All three go. The parent list is also unigram-only and correctly omits liability, which is neutral in a financial statement. The new list adds bigrams such as product liability, environmental liability, false advertising, and filed suit, which carry the meaning that the single word does not. For a marketing reader, the dictionary is in part a list of marketing-made obligations: false advertising, deceptive, product liability, recall, warranty defect, counterfeit, unfair competition.

How to weight. Every term counts equally. The cited justification is a comparison of methods in the disclosure literature, which finds equal-weighted, domain-specific word counts about as powerful as more elaborate schemes, provided the list excludes words that also appear in other contexts (Henry and Leone 2016). That is why so much of the effort goes into pruning.

How to scale. The main measure is the log of the raw count, with the log of filing length entered as a control. The authors argue against the usual share-of-words scaling. In sentiment work every word is positive, negative, or neutral, so a share is natural. Here the researcher is looking for one kind of content inside a document that is mostly about other things, and dividing by length lets differences in length drive the variation. Where a control is impossible, as in portfolio sorts, they fall back on the share.

The scaling decision has consequences that a short simulation makes visible. In their Table 3 the coefficient of the log count on log filing length is about 1.2, so dictionary hits grow faster than the filing does. The simulation below builds that in. It is our illustration and uses no data from the paper. Each filing has a latent exposure that the researcher never sees, a length, and a count of dictionary hits that depends on both. The outcome depends on exposure and, separately and negatively, on length.

Code
# A stylized illustration written for this section; none of it is the paper's data.
set.seed(41)
n      <- 20000
theta  <- rnorm(n)                         # latent exposure, never observed
len    <- 10 + 0.74 * rnorm(n)             # log words in the filing
count  <- rpois(n, exp(4.3 + 0.5 * theta + 1.2 * (len - 10)))   # dictionary hits
y      <- 1.0 * theta - 0.5 * (len - 10) + rnorm(n, sd = 3)     # long filings do worse

z <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(x))
log_count <- log(1 + count)
share     <- count / exp(len)
resid_ct  <- resid(lm(log_count ~ len))    # log count net of filing length

slope <- function(f) unname(coef(lm(f))[2])
scaling <- data.frame(
  measure = c("Log count, no length control", "Share of total words",
              "Log count, length controlled", "Latent exposure (infeasible)"),
  cor_with_exposure = c(cor(log_count, theta), cor(share, theta),
                        cor(resid_ct, theta), 1),
  cor_with_length   = c(cor(log_count, len), cor(share, len),
                        cor(resid_ct, len), cor(theta, len)),
  slope_per_sd      = c(slope(y ~ z(log_count)), slope(y ~ z(share)),
                        slope(y ~ z(resid_ct) + len), slope(y ~ z(theta) + len))
)
scaling[-1] <- round(scaling[-1], 2)
print(scaling, row.names = FALSE)
#>                       measure cor_with_exposure cor_with_length slope_per_sd
#>  Log count, no length control              0.48            0.86         0.14
#>          Share of total words              0.87            0.26         0.74
#>  Log count, length controlled              0.96            0.00         0.92
#>  Latent exposure (infeasible)              1.00            0.00         0.96

The raw log count is mostly a measure of how long the filing is, and its slope on the outcome is close to zero because the length effect cancels the exposure effect. The share does much better, but it still loads on length, because hits grow faster than words, and it recovers only about three-quarters of the true slope. The log count with length controlled comes close to the infeasible benchmark. Two things follow for anyone building a count-based measure. Estimate the elasticity of the count to document length before choosing a scaling, since a share is right only when that elasticity is one. And when two versions of the measure appear in one paper, say which result rests on which.

76.13.4 The validation ladder

The paper never claims that its dictionary is accurate. It shows, one test at a time, that the measure sits where the construct should sit among other variables. That is a nomological argument (Section 39.4), and laid out as a ladder it reads as follows.

Four features of the ladder are worth copying beyond the list itself.

  1. The outcomes come from somewhere else. Lawsuits come from a law-school clearinghouse, reputation from a commercial media-screening vendor, and returns from the exchange. None of them is built from 10-K text, so the measure cannot predict them by construction.
  2. Every test is run twice, across firms and within firm. The within-firm version says that when a firm’s own filings add liability language, lawsuits and bad press follow. That answers the objection that the measure only identifies a type of firm.
  3. The descriptive tables are allowed to disagree with the thesis. In the raw quintile means, valuation ratios rise with IL. The negative relation appears only once size, profitability, and industry are held fixed. The authors print the raw table, say that it shows a positive association, and then show the regression. A referee who finds that reversal unaided will distrust the paper. A referee who is told about it will not.
  4. The pricing result is given a reason. A return premium invites the charge of data mining (Section 26.9.1). The paper answers with a risk story, that these liabilities can crystallize suddenly, and tests an implication of the story on a different outcome, crash risk. It then tests the rival story, mispricing, on earnings announcements, and concedes that the two cannot be fully separated.

76.13.5 Opening the authors’ data: what the term counts show

The paper’s replication package, available from the journal’s supplemental-material page, includes the count of every dictionary term in every filing, together with the Stata logs behind each table. The return, accounting, and reputation data are licensed and not included, so the regressions cannot be rerun from the package alone. Two checks are still possible. The first is against the logs. They reproduce the means and standard deviations in the manuscript’s descriptive table, and the twelve portfolio alphas to within 0.03 percentage points, so the estimates quoted in this section match the authors’ final runs. The second is on the measure itself. The script replication/intangible-liabilities/il_measure_checks.R in this book’s repository computes the statistics below from the term counts, over all 232,874 filings from 32,604 filers with fiscal years 1996 to 2020. That is the full set of filings scored, about twice the 112,457 firm-years that survive the match to stock and accounting data, so the figures describe the measure before any sample selection. They are our calculations and appear nowhere in the paper.

Three lessons follow, and each one is a check any dictionary paper can run on itself.

A dictionary of 569 terms is, in use, a dictionary of about 50. Zipf’s law guarantees that a few frequent terms dominate any count. The ten that dominate here are the most generic words on the list, and legal appears in nearly every filing. The measure survives their removal almost unchanged, which is reassuring, and it is the kind of evidence a reader wants in the paper: a table of the top terms with their share of hits, and the measure recomputed without them.

A sub-construct can be nearly invisible inside the total. The marketing-made obligations are in the dictionary, but they carry 1.4% of the count and move largely independently of it. A researcher who wants product-harm or false-advertising exposure should build that index separately and validate it separately. The full measure is mostly a litigation-and-contingency measure.

Check the named cases under both scalings. The paper contrasts IBM, with very low intangible liabilities, and HP, with very high ones. In the fiscal-2020 counts HP has 767 hits in a filing of about 52,800 words and IBM has 77 in a filing of about 10,300 words. On the raw log count IBM sits at the 15th percentile of that year’s filings and HP at the 96th. Net of length, year, and industry, IBM rises to the 79th percentile and HP stays at the 95th. IBM’s 10-K is short, which is what one would see if much of its annual report were incorporated by reference in exhibits that the text processing drops, though the package cannot confirm the reason. The other named cases hold either way: 3M, PG&E, and Corteva are above the 90th percentile on both versions, and Boston Beer is below the 15th on both. An illustrative contrast should be chosen after checking that it does not depend on the scaling.

76.13.6 Where the specimen is thin

A template is more useful with its weak points marked, and several of them are places where a marketing referee would press harder than a finance referee did.

  • No human has checked the measure against text. There is no hand-coded sample of filings, no precision for individual terms, and no test of whether a high score means much liability or much boilerplate. The generic words that dominate the count (Table 76.19) appear in filings with nothing at stake. The validation is entirely by association with outcomes. A marketing journal would normally ask for agreement with human judgment as well (Section 47.5.2).
  • The simplest rival is beaten off the page. A footnote reports that the parent dictionary shows no robust relation to future lawsuits, reputation, or returns. This is the comparison that justifies all the pruning, and it is described as unreported. It should be a table (Section 76.9 makes the same point about method papers).
  • The legal outcome is narrower than the construct. The lawsuits are securities class actions, which shareholders bring. The construct’s own examples are product, environmental, and intellectual-property claims. The two are related, since a product disaster often triggers a shareholder suit, but the validation outcome is not the obligation the paper defines.
  • Filing length does a lot of work. Adding length and three accounting ratios lifts the explained variance of IL from 0.51 to 0.75. In the return regressions, length carries a coefficient of \(-0.17\) beside IL’s \(+0.16\). The finding is therefore about liability language relative to the length of the filing, and long filings alone predict lower returns. The simulation above shows why this must be stated plainly, and the IBM case shows it in the data.
  • The headline number is one of several. The abstract’s 3% matches the industry-adjusted figures (a 3.02% return spread and a 2.99% six-factor alpha). The same table gives 2.11%, significant only at the 10% level, under the industry-adjusted \(q^5\) model and 6.02% under a mispricing-factor model. Announcement returns for high-IL firms are significantly negative in the two specifications without industry effects and insignificant with them.
  • The predictive words are hard to read. The LASSO’s 149 selected terms include infringement, product liability, and fraud, and also majeure, bailiff, and attornment. The text describes a pre-2015 training sample and a post-2015 test sample but reports no out-of-sample fit. The authors do warn that a zero coefficient does not make a word uninformative.
  • Some counts do not reconcile in the manuscript. The text gives 112,716 firm-years and the descriptive table 112,457. The package’s construction log settles it in favor of the table: 114,276 filings match the stock and accounting data, and 1,819 without a count are dropped. The reputation sample is 11,329 in the text and 11,256 or 12,598 in the regressions. The final typeset version may resolve these. The lesson from Section 76.12 applies here too: every sample size in the prose should be recomputable from a table.

None of this undoes the contribution. It marks what a successor paper can add, and the authors’ own conclusion lists two of the items: more sources (earnings calls, social media, press coverage) and better language models.

76.13.7 Carrying the template into a marketing journal

Marketing is full of constructs that firms describe in words and no database records. A firm’s exposure to a product-harm crisis, its dependence on a few customers or one retailer, its reliance on a celebrity or founder, its privacy and data-breach exposure, and the gap between its sustainability claims and its operations are all discussed in filings, earnings calls, complaints, and reviews, and none has a standard variable. One of the authors had already applied the recipe on the asset side, with a brand measure built from the frequency of the word brand in filings (Boustanifar and Kang 2025) (Chapter 12). Seen together, the two papers are one research program: pick an off-balance-sheet quantity, find the text in which firms must discuss it, count, validate, and price.

Four adjustments help a marketing version.

  • Validate against people as well as outcomes. Have trained coders rate a few hundred documents on the construct, report agreement among them, and report how the measure tracks their ratings. Predictive tests show that a measure is useful. Agreement with human judgment shows that it measures what its name says (Section 39.4).
  • Tabulate the horse race. Put the parent dictionary, a share-scaled version, an embedding-expanded dictionary (Section 47.4.2), and an LLM coder (Section 47.6) in one table with the same outcomes. If the simple count wins or ties, transparency is the argument for it. If it loses, the paper has a better measure.
  • Choose outcomes a marketing reader prices. Recalls, regulatory actions, complaint volume, brand-tracking scores, customer churn, and retailer delistings can play the role that class actions and RepRisk play here. Stock returns remain available for a strategy audience (Chapter 26).
  • Decide what the last third of the paper is. A finance paper ends with pricing. A marketing paper can end with a decision instead: which firms should change disclosure, product design, or claims, and what it is worth to them. If the measured facts raise a question that reduced-form evidence cannot settle, a small model is the other way to finish (Section 76.3.4).
A checklist for the measurement paper
  1. Name the construct by its relation to one the field already measures, and define it with a rule that says what is in and what is out.
  2. Open with a named case in which the standard data record nothing and the stakes are plainly large.
  3. Explain who produces the source text, under what obligation, and with what incentive to distort it.
  4. Start from a published instrument. Document deletions and additions with examples, and print the full instrument in an appendix.
  5. Estimate how the raw count scales with document length before choosing between a share and a controlled count, and say which results use which.
  6. Show that the measure sorts known groups and finds known cases, then report how much variance those groups leave unexplained.
  7. Predict future outcomes drawn from independent sources, across units and within unit.
  8. Tie the measure to a price or a decision.
  9. Put the nearest existing measures, and the parent instrument, in the same table. Report the top terms’ share of the count and the measure recomputed without them.
  10. Validate against human coding as well as against outcomes.
  11. Show where in the source the signal sits and which terms carry it, with out-of-sample fit.
  12. Print the raw descriptive pattern even when it runs against the conditional one, and make every sample size recomputable.

76.14 The Front End

The front end—title, abstract, and introduction—is the part of the paper most people read and the only part most people read. It carries the entire promise– payoff loop of Figure 76.1 in compressed form, and a reviewer’s accept-lean or reject-lean is often set before the methods section begins. The front end deserves a disproportionate share of writing effort precisely because it does a disproportionate share of the persuasive work.

76.14.1 The title

A title’s job is to name the contribution in eight to fifteen words such that the right reader stops scrolling. It should contain the paper’s key constructs (the terms a searcher would type) and, where possible, signal the relationship the paper establishes rather than merely the topic it addresses. “Brand Prominence and Status Signaling” names a topic; “Signaling Status with Luxury Goods: The Role of Brand Prominence” names a relationship and a mechanism. Question titles and two-part titles (a hook before the colon, the substance after) are common in JCR and JM and rarer in Marketing Science, reflecting the venues’ different house voices—a difference worth matching to the target journal.

76.14.2 The abstract

The abstract is the most-read and least-revised 250 words in science, and the imbalance is a mistake. It must be self-contained: a reader who sees only the abstract should be able to state the paper’s objective, method, principal finding, and implication. The canonical structure mirrors Equation 76.1 in miniature—one or two sentences each for the problem, the approach, the result (with direction and, where it fits, magnitude), and the “so what”. Two failure modes dominate. The descriptive abstract announces what the paper does (“we examine the effect of X on Y”) without ever stating what it found, leaving the reader no wiser; the overloaded abstract crams in every robustness check and moderator, drowning the headline. The fix for both is the same: lead with the finding.

76.14.3 The introduction as a funnel

The introduction is where most rejections are decided, and it has a near-mechanical structure: a funnel from the broad problem to the specific contribution. A robust template runs problem \(\rightarrow\) tension or puzzle \(\rightarrow\) gap \(\rightarrow\) “in this paper we” \(\rightarrow\) approach \(\rightarrow\) findings \(\rightarrow\) contributions \(\rightarrow\) roadmap. Figure 76.11 renders it.

Two discipline points govern the funnel. First, the pivot sentence—“In this paper, we…”—should arrive early, by the end of the second page; an introduction that is still motivating the problem on page four has lost the reviewer. Second, the contributions should be stated as claims the reader will be able to accept, not as activities the authors performed. “We contribute by examining the role of arousal” is an activity; “We show that empathetic responses raise gratitude even before a service failure is resolved, which the prior literature’s resolution-centric models cannot accommodate” is a claim and an explicit \(\Delta\mathcal{K}\).

76.14.4 Positioning against the literature

The literature review is not a homage to everyone who has touched the topic; it is the construction of \(\mathcal{K}_{\text{before}}\), the precise baseline against which the contribution is measured. Its house failure mode is the annotated bibliography—a serial list of “Author (year) found X; Author (year) found Y”—which demonstrates reading but not synthesis and leaves the reviewer to infer the gap. The remedy is to organize the review around tensions and open questions rather than around papers, so that the gap emerges as the natural next move in a conversation the reader can now follow. The house style guide’s instruction to weave, not list citations is exactly this principle applied at the sentence level: each citation should earn its place by advancing the argument, and the strongest evidence per point should crowd out the duplicative.

76.15 Writing for the Top-4

76.15.1 What rises to a top journal

The top-4 differ from solid field journals less in the correctness of the work they publish than in the size and generality of the increment \(\Delta\mathcal{K}\). The bar that rises is importance: a top-4 paper must change how a non-trivial slice of the field thinks, not merely add a brick to a narrow wall. Editors and reviewers operationalize this in recurring questions—Would I assign this in a doctoral seminar? Does it change what I would tell a manager? Does it open new research, or close a question others were pursuing? A paper can be flawless and still be rejected for answering a question too few people were asking.

The venues also have distinguishable identities, and matching the paper to the venue is part of the craft. Marketing Science and JMR lean toward methodological rigor and formal models—a structural estimator or an analytical game-theoretic result is at home there. JCR prizes psychological process and theory, typically established across multiple experiments that triangulate a mechanism. JM spans substantive and managerial questions with an explicit demand for managerial relevance. The same finding, dressed for the wrong venue, draws reviewers who want what the paper was never built to deliver.

76.15.2 Genres of contribution: many roads to the top-4

The importance bar is not cleared in a single way. Marketing is methodologically plural, and a top journal publishes several distinct genres of research, each with its own logic of contribution and its own standard of proof. Naming the genre—to oneself first, then to the reader—matters as much as naming the paper type earlier in this chapter, because a reviewer recruited for one genre will judge by its rules. A working map of the traditions a marketing scholar will meet:

  • Experimental and consumer-behavior work identifies a psychological mechanism by controlled manipulation, usually triangulated across several studies that close off rival accounts one at a time. The contribution is a process: not merely that \(X\) moves \(Y\) but why.
  • Analytical / game-theoretic work builds a deliberately stylized model and extracts a non-obvious, general implication from its equilibrium—why a firm might rationally do the counterintuitive thing. The currency is generality, not data.
  • Empirical / structural work estimates the primitives of behavior—preferences, costs—under an explicit identification argument so it can run counterfactuals the raw data never ran (Section 38.4). The contribution is policy-relevant quantities and the “what if” they license.
  • Descriptive work documents robust, previously unseen patterns in novel—often large-scale—data, and makes no causal claim. The contribution is the fact itself.
  • Prescriptive / optimization work formulates a decision problem and solves it with a guarantee or a demonstrably better method (Section 38.4.1). The contribution is a solvable formulation and its performance.
  • Strategy and marketing-management work links a marketing action to firm outcomes and firm value with an explicit demand for managerial relevance (the JM register above).

These are axes, not bins: a single paper is often empirical and descriptive, or analytical and prescriptive, and the strongest work borrows across them. But the reader must be told which claim bears the weight, because the standard of proof differs by genre—an identification argument is decisive for a structural paper and beside the point for an analytical one.

The genre students most often underrate is the descriptive, and it repays a closer look because its revival is one of the field’s live developments. For two decades the credibility revolution (Section 77.8) so prized causal identification that pure description read as second class—a table on the way to a regression. That has reversed, for a concrete reason: platform, transaction, and sensor data now expose patterns no prior dataset could show, and a pattern no one had seen is a genuine increment to \(\mathcal{K}\) even with no causal arrow attached. The descriptive paper still clears the top-4 bar, but on different terms. It does not owe internal validity for an effect it never claims; it owes (i) genuinely novel data, (ii) patterns robust to how the data are sliced, (iii) a surprise—a fact that overturns or sharpens a belief the field held—and (iv) scrupulous candor about what is described versus explained. Overclaiming causation is the descriptive paper’s characteristic failure; under-selling importance (“we merely describe”) is its mirror-image one.

Chen and Xiang (2026) is a clean specimen. From millions of cross-border orders the authors document a U-shaped relationship between income and counterfeit consumption—both low- and high-income consumers buy more fakes than the middle, with the tails differing in composition—advancing no instrument and estimating no treatment effect. Its title announces “A Descriptive Analysis,” and its contribution is precisely the documented gradient, which complicates the tidy poseur account of counterfeit demand (Chapter 12). That the top journals now run short-format Frontiers articles for exactly this kind of high-value description—Kaiser and Schulze (2026)’s map of a nascent LLM sales channel is a companion case—is institutional evidence that the genre has a settled place. The craft lesson mirrors the framing discipline of Section 76.2: know your genre, promise the kind of contribution it actually makes, and defend it on its own terms rather than borrowing the rhetoric of a genre you did not practice.

Chang et al. (2026) is a second specimen, and a useful complement because it ran as a full article without the Frontiers label, and because almost every design choice in it is visible from its front matter. The question is small and concrete: do online home listings with more pictures of plants sell for more? From 40,294 sold properties and their 569,773 listing photos on a major U.S. real-estate platform, labelled for plant content by a multimodal language model, the authors document that listings with more plant imagery transact at higher prices, sell faster, and attract more online engagement, after accounting for an extensive set of property, neighborhood, listing, and market factors. Six choices are worth copying.

  1. The title names the genre, and the claim never borrows a causal verb. The one-sentence summary on the journal record says plant imagery is “associated with” higher valuations. A reader is told what kind of evidence to expect before reading a single table, which pre-empts the “where is the instrument?” review.
  2. Theory motivates the look without being put on trial. Phytophilia, the idea that people are innately drawn to plant life, explains why anyone should expect a pattern. The paper does not claim to test it, and does not need to.
  3. A practitioner survey supplies the surprise. The authors survey real-estate agents and report that awareness of plants as a staging tool, and the priority agents give it, are low. That converts a correlation into a fact worth knowing: the pattern is valuable precisely because the people who could act on it do not act on it. It is the descriptive paper’s version of the “open question” of Section 76.2.3.
  4. Several outcomes, one direction. Price, time on market, and online engagement are three outcomes with different confounds. A pattern that runs the same way in all three is harder to explain away than a pattern in one, and triangulation of this kind does part of the work that a mechanism test does in a causal paper.
  5. The conditioning set is the robustness argument. The obvious rival account is that greenery proxies for bigger lots, richer neighborhoods, better photographers, and more effort by the seller. A descriptive paper cannot rule that account out with exogenous variation, so it narrows it with controls for property, neighborhood, listing, and market factors, and states that what survives is an association.
  6. Measurement is the method. A general-purpose vision-language model makes a narrow visual construct codable at a scale no research assistant could match (Chapter 49). The paper’s reference list (manual image-annotation software, CLIP, Faster R-CNN, VGG, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5) points to a pipeline built with manual annotation and several competing models. Its validation is where a reader should look first, because a generated label is the one input a descriptive design cannot afford to get wrong.

The paper also cites de Kadt and Grzymala-Busse (2025), whose standard is a useful checklist for anyone writing in this genre: a good descriptive question uncovers a fact in need of explanation, builds theory, or helps evaluate theory, and a good descriptive analysis is clear, comparable, and complete. Filled in for this paper, the contribution sentence of Section 76.2 reads: we establish that listing photos with more plants are associated with higher prices, faster sales, and more engagement among U.S. homes, a pattern prior work could not document because coding plants in half a million photos was too costly, and one practitioners do not act on.

76.15.3 Robustness as rhetoric

At the top-4, a single clean result rarely suffices; the paper must anticipate and preempt the reviewer’s alternative explanations. This is why top-4 empirical papers carry batteries of robustness checks, alternative specifications, and—in experimental work—multiple studies whose designs rule out competing accounts one by one. The logic is the broken-arrow logic of Equation 76.1: every alternative explanation is a way the arrow \(D \Rightarrow R\) might fail, and each robustness check is a patch that keeps the arrow intact. The writing task is to present this defensive machinery without burying the headline—typically by stating the main result cleanly, then organizing the defenses as a navigable sequence of named threats and the evidence that disarms each.

The reviewer is not your enemy; the reviewer is the proxy for every skeptical reader your paper will ever have. Every alternative explanation a reviewer raises is one a future reader would have raised silently and then disbelieved you. Writing the rebuttal into the paper before submission is simply doing the reviewer’s job for them, and it is the single highest-return revision activity.

76.15.4 The review process and the response

Top-4 papers are essentially never accepted on first submission; the modal good outcome is a revise and resubmit (R&R), and the revision is where many papers are won or lost. The response to reviewers is itself a document with its own craft. Its governing principle is that the author’s job is to make the editor’s accept-decision easy to defend: every reviewer comment receives a numbered, verbatim restatement followed by a specific response and a pointer to the exact change in the manuscript. Disagreement is permitted but must be argued with evidence, courteously, and sparingly—an author who fights every point signals defensiveness, while an author who concedes everything signals that the original work was unconsidered. The art is to distinguish comments that improve the paper (adopt them) from comments that reflect a misunderstanding (clarify the text so the next reader does not misunderstand either) from the rare comment that is simply wrong (rebut it with evidence and grace).

76.16 Clarity and Revision

76.16.1 Clarity as a property of the reader, not the writer

Clarity is not an ornament; it is the probability that a reader recovers the intended meaning on the first pass. Writing that the author finds clear because the author already knows the answer is a category error—the test of clarity is whether a reader who does not yet know the conclusion can follow the argument. A few sentence-level disciplines do most of the work, and they are mechanical enough to apply as a checklist. Prefer the active voice and a concrete agent (“we estimate”, “the model predicts”) over agentless passives that hide who did what. Put the subject and verb early and close together so the reader is not made to hold an open clause across half a line. Use one term for one concept—do not alternate “effect”, “impact”, and “influence” for the same quantity, because the reader will hunt for a distinction that is not there. Expand every acronym on first use and define every construct before deploying it, a discipline the house style enforces throughout.

76.16.2 Measuring readability

Readability can be measured, and while no formula substitutes for judgment, the indices make a useful diagnostic. The Gunning fog index estimates the years of formal education a reader needs to understand a passage on first reading (Gunning et al. 1952). Let a passage contain \(W\) words, \(S\) sentences, and \(C\) “complex” words (three or more syllables, excluding common suffix inflections). The index is

\[ \text{Fog} \;=\; 0.4\left(\frac{W}{S} \;+\; 100\,\frac{C}{W}\right), \tag{76.5}\]

a weighted sum of average sentence length and the percentage of complex words. The two terms encode the two main sources of difficulty—long sentences and unfamiliar words—and the constant scales the result to a U.S. grade level, so a fog score of 12 corresponds roughly to the reading level of a high-school senior. Academic prose runs higher, but a methods section with a fog score in the high teens is usually not “rigorous”; it is merely overlong in the sentence and overloaded in the noun phrase. Textual-complexity measures of exactly this family are now standard tools in the marketing and finance literatures for analyzing corporate disclosures and other documents at scale (Loughran and McDonald 2024, 2020), which is a useful reminder that the readability of your prose is itself a measurable, and therefore improvable, quantity.

The estimator in Equation 76.5 is a heuristic, not a model, and its assumptions are worth stating because they tell you when it misleads. It assumes that syllable count proxies word difficulty (false for short technical jargon like “prior” or “yield”, which are hard despite being monosyllabic) and that sentence length proxies syntactic load (false for a long but perfectly parallel list). It is best read as a smoke detector: a high score reliably indicates a problem somewhere, but a low score does not certify clarity. The following chunk implements it and a companion length diagnostic so the measure is reproducible rather than mystical; Figure 76.12 shows the score falling as the same sentence is progressively tightened.

Code
set.seed(41)

# A deliberately rough syllable counter: count vowel groups per word.
# Heuristic, not linguistic ground truth -- adequate for a relative diagnostic.
count_syllables <- function(word) {
  word <- tolower(gsub("[^a-z]", "", word))
  if (nchar(word) == 0) return(0L)
  groups <- gregexpr("[aeiouy]+", word)[[1]]
  n <- if (groups[1] == -1L) 1L else length(groups)
  if (grepl("e$", word) && n > 1L) n <- n - 1L   # silent terminal 'e'
  max(n, 1L)
}

gunning_fog <- function(text) {
  sentences <- unlist(strsplit(text, "(?<=[.!?])\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  sentences <- sentences[nzchar(trimws(sentences))]
  words <- unlist(strsplit(text, "\\s+"))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  W <- length(words); S <- max(length(sentences), 1L)
  syl <- vapply(words, count_syllables, integer(1))
  C <- sum(syl >= 3L)                              # "complex" words
  0.4 * (W / S + 100 * C / W)
}

versions <- c(
  bloated  = paste("The utilization of an excessively elaborate and",
                   "circumlocutory prose style, characterized by the",
                   "accumulation of subordinate clauses, demonstrably",
                   "attenuates comprehensibility for the readership."),
  moderate = paste("Using an elaborate, indirect prose style with many",
                   "subordinate clauses reduces how well readers understand",
                   "the argument."),
  lean     = "Dense prose is hard to read."
)

fog <- vapply(versions, gunning_fog, numeric(1))
print(round(fog, 1))
#>  bloated moderate     lean 
#>     28.3     20.9      2.4

barplot(fog, col = "grey80", border = NA, ylab = "Gunning fog (grade level)",
        main = "Readability across three drafts of one claim",
        names.arg = names(versions))
abline(h = 12, lty = 2)

76.16.3 Revision as a process

First drafts are for the writer; revision is for the reader. The empirical regularity behind all writing advice is that meaning is discovered, not transcribed: the act of writing reveals which arrows in Equation 76.1 are actually weak, and the first draft’s value is largely diagnostic. Productive revision proceeds top-down— structure before paragraph, paragraph before sentence, sentence before word—because fixing a comma in a paragraph that will be deleted is wasted effort. A useful sequence is to first verify that the contribution sentence is present and true, then that each section answers its one question, then that each paragraph has a single point announced in its first sentence, and only then to polish prose. The “reverse outline”—reading the draft and writing in the margin the single claim each paragraph makes—exposes structural defects (two paragraphs making the same point, a claim with no supporting paragraph, a paragraph with no claim) that are invisible at the sentence level.

A final discipline is distance. Prose that seems clear the night it is written is frequently opaque a week later, when the author has forgotten the unstated assumptions that made it cohere—and a week-later author is a closer proxy for the real reader than the night-of author ever is. Where time does not permit distance, a co-author or colleague reading cold is the next best instrument, and the most valuable feedback is not “I disagree” but “I got lost here”, because confusion localizes a broken arrow that the author can no longer see.

76.17 Key Takeaways

  • A paper is a reconstructed argument, not a lab diary: the order of exposition is engineered for the reader, and each section answers exactly one question with its own default verb tense (Table 76.1).
  • The effect–mechanism–boundary architecture answers whether, how, and for whom in that order, and the method must change at each stage because the question does—quasi-experimental for the average effect, structural equations for the pathway, set-theoretic for the configurations (Section 76.6). Put the robustness where identification is weakest, and state plainly that identification strength declines from stage to stage. The test of whether the later stages are contributions rather than decoration is whether a null there would have changed the paper (Singh et al. 2026).
  • A design-science method paper hangs on its design framework, which maps goals to challenges and gives each challenge exactly one component (Table 76.12). It evaluates the method at three levels: model, application, and mechanism. Its mechanism evidence is ablation plus a direct check of the property each component claims, and its simplest credible rival is the heuristic version of its own idea (Wang et al. 2026; Xu et al. 2026).
  • A theory-building paper names a construct from data in which hidden behavior was forced into the open. It defines the construct from an existing concept, splits it into parts a coder can find, states the boundary where it stops applying, sorts its forms along one dimension, and derives remedies from the mechanism (Table 76.15). Every headline number should be recomputable from a table in the paper (Weiss and Radoynovska 2026a).
  • The argument is a chain of claims the reader may refuse to grant (Equation 76.1); a paper fails at its weakest arrow, and most “low contribution” rejections are in fact broken arrows—a filled gap or a design that cannot license the conclusion.
  • Motivate with a question, not a gap. The strongest setup assembles two established literatures that imply opposite answers, or that block both obvious remedies, so that no informed reader can guess the result—human bias and machine bias doing exactly that in Tanlamai, Khern-am-nuai, and Cohen (2026) (Section 76.2.3). Write it so both branches are publishable before you know which one you have; remember that a counter-intuitive finding raises the evidentiary bar and obligates a real mechanism section; and state each literature’s position in terms its own authors would sign.
  • A contribution is the warranted increment to knowledge \(\Delta\mathcal{K}\) (Equation 76.2); it must be novel, valid, and important, and the top-4 bar that rises is importance. State the most general claim the evidence licenses, and not one inch more.
  • The front end carries the promise; the discussion must redeem exactly that promise. Make the “in this paper, we…” pivot early and state contributions as claims, not activities (Figure 76.11).
  • Not every paper is hypo-deductive. A descriptive paper contributes a pattern and names its ceiling; an abductive paper reasons from the pattern to the best explanation and owes the reader the whole candidate set (Equation 76.3). The PEEBI structure—priors, establish, evaluate, best explanation, implication (Table 76.5)—reports that reasoning honestly where the deductive template would force a fiction about the order of discovery.
  • A new measure earns a top-journal contribution when its facts carry a price and pose a question they cannot answer alone. When a null outcome gap could be a true zero or a real effect masked by selected adoption, a small model disciplined by the measured facts, and identified by a moment the headline facts do not use, turns the null into a statement about motives: many start-ups advertise a worker-centered culture mainly to save on wages (Lee 2026) (Section 76.3.4).
  • A measurement paper contributes a variable, and its regressions exist to earn trust in that variable. Define the construct with a rule, explain why the source must contain it, start from a published instrument and print the new one, then climb a validation ladder from known groups to independent future outcomes to prices (Table 76.18). Check how a count scales with document length before choosing a scaling, and validate against human coding as well as outcomes (Boustanifar and Verriest 2026) (Section 76.13).
  • Robustness is rhetoric: writing the reviewer’s objections into the paper before submission is the highest-return revision activity, and the R&R response is a craft document whose job is to make the editor’s decision easy to defend.
  • Clarity is a property of the reader: measure it (Equation 76.5), revise top-down from structure to sentence, and use distance or a cold reader to localize the arrows you can no longer see are broken.

76.18 Further Reading

For the structure of scientific argument and the discipline of revision, the classic writing-craft literature is the natural starting point; for the specific norms of the marketing top-4, the editorials and “from the editor” notes of JM, JMR, Marketing Science, and JCR are the authoritative—and frequently updated— statements of what each venue rewards. The On the reporting of non-deductive work, Pillai et al. (2026) is the direct statement of the PEEBI structure and Pillai, Goldfarb, and Kirsch (2024) the companion treatment of what makes one explanation better than another; Choudhury, Moeen, and Wormald (2026) supplies the design-side account of abduction that the two SMJ papers presuppose. Read together they are the closest thing the field has to a manual for writing a paper whose conclusion was discovered rather than predicted.

For the design-science method paper, Hevner et al. (2004) set out the guidelines that IS referees still apply, and Gregor and Hevner (2013) explain how to position and state a design contribution, from an instantiated artifact up to a design theory. Abbasi et al. (2024) is the ISR editors’ statement of what they now expect from AI-based design research.

The textual-analysis methods that let us measure the readability of our own and others’ prose are developed in the disclosure literature (Loughran and McDonald 2024, 2020) and connect this chapter to the broader treatment of text as data elsewhere in the book.

75  Writing the Policy-and-Welfare Paper for Marketing Journals
77  The Review Process
Source Code
# Scientific Writing {#sec-scientific-writing}

A research paper is the instrument through which a discovery becomes knowledge.
A result that is not written down does not exist scientifically; a result written
badly exists only for the handful of readers willing to excavate it. This chapter
treats scientific writing not as cosmetic polish applied after the "real" work but
as an integral part of the research itself—a design problem with its own
constraints, its own failure modes, and its own measurable quality. The audience
is the marketing scholar who has a finding and now faces the harder task of
convincing a skeptical editor, two or three adversarial reviewers, and an
indifferent field that the finding is correct, novel, and important.

The economics of the situation are unforgiving. The top journals in marketing—the
*Journal of Marketing* (JM), the *Journal of Marketing Research* (JMR),
*Marketing Science*, and the *Journal of Consumer Research* (JCR), collectively
the "top-4"—desk-reject a large share of submissions and ultimately accept only a
small fraction of what is sent to them. <!-- CITE-NEEDED: top-4 marketing journal acceptance/desk-reject rates -->
A reviewer reads dozens of papers a year as unpaid labor and forms a judgment
within the first few pages. The paper that survives is not merely the one with the
best result; it is the one whose argument the reviewer can reconstruct without
effort and whose contribution the reviewer can state in a sentence. Writing is
therefore a competitive technology, and this chapter develops it as one.

The chapter proceeds from architecture to sentence. We begin with the **structure**
of a paper—the canonical section sequence and what each section is for—and formalize
the underlying logical scaffold. We then treat the hardest and most consequential
task, **framing the contribution**, and then the two genres the hypo-deductive
template serves badly—the **descriptive paper**, which contributes a pattern, and
the **abductive paper**, which reasons from a pattern to the best available
explanation. Next comes the part of the paper where framing
lives or dies: the **front end** (title, abstract, introduction). We turn next to
the specific demands of writing for the **top-4**, where the contribution bar is
highest. We close with **clarity and revision**: the sentence-level craft that
makes an argument legible, the measurement of readability, and the disciplined
process of responding to reviewers. Throughout, the stance is the house stance—
intuition first, then the formal structure that makes the intuition operational.

## The Structure of a Paper {#sec-sw-structure}

### The canonical sections and their tenses

Empirical marketing papers share a near-universal skeleton, sometimes abbreviated
**IMRaD** (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) with literature review
and conclusions bracketing the core. Each section answers one question and only
one, and—this is a point novices routinely miss—each section has a *default verb
tense* that signals the epistemic status of its claims. Completed actions take the
**simple past** ("we estimated", "respondents rated"); established knowledge and
the paper's own ongoing argument take the **present** ("the effect is", "Table 2
reports"); prior literature as a stream that continues into the present takes the
**present perfect** ("researchers have shown"). @tbl-sw-sections collects the
sections, their purposes, approximate lengths, and tense conventions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sw-sections
#| tbl-cap: "Canonical sections of an empirical marketing paper, with purpose, indicative length, and default verb tense. Lengths are rules of thumb for a full-length top-4 submission, not hard limits."
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(knitr)
sw_sections <- data.frame(
  Section = c("Title", "Abstract", "Introduction", "Literature / Theory",
              "Methods", "Results", "Discussion", "Conclusion"),
  `Words` = c("8–15", "200–250", "800–1200", "1500–3000",
              "1000–2500", "1000–2500", "1500–2500", "400–800"),
  Purpose = c("Name the contribution",
              "Self-contained summary: objective, method, finding, implication",
              "Why the paper exists; the gap and the contribution",
              "Position vs. prior work; derive hypotheses or model",
              "What was done, reproducibly",
              "What was found, with the data doing the talking",
              "What it means, limits, boundary conditions",
              "Restate contribution; implications and future work"),
  `Default tense` = c("—", "Past + present", "Present + present perfect",
                      "Present + present perfect", "Past", "Past + present",
                      "Present + past", "Present"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(sw_sections)
```

The discipline of one-question-per-section is what gives a paper its navigability.
A reader who wants to know *what you did* turns to Methods and finds only that; a
reader who wants to know *why it matters* turns to the Discussion and is not
detained by procedure. Violations—results smuggled into the methods, mechanism
speculation buried in the results—are the most common structural defect flagged in
review, because they force the reader to hold the paper's logic in their head
rather than read it off the page.

> A scientific paper is not a chronological record of what the researcher did. It
> is a reconstructed argument, organized so that the reader can verify the
> conclusion with minimum effort. The order of discovery and the order of
> exposition are different things, and conflating them is the surest route to an
> unreadable manuscript.

### The argument as a logical object

Underneath the section skeleton sits a logical scaffold that the prose merely
dresses. Make it explicit. A confirmatory empirical paper advances a chain

$$
\underbrace{P}_{\text{problem}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{G}_{\text{gap}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{H}_{\text{hypotheses}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{D}_{\text{design}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{R}_{\text{results}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{C}_{\text{contribution}}
$$ {#eq-sw-chain}

in which every arrow is a claim the reader can refuse to grant. The problem $P$
must be real (someone cares about the answer); the gap $G$ must be genuine (the
answer is not already known); the hypotheses $H$ must follow from a theory and be
falsifiable; the design $D$ must be capable of discriminating $H$ from its
negation; the results $R$ must actually bear on $H$; and the contribution $C$ must
be what $R$ licenses, not more. A paper fails at whichever arrow is weakest, and
the writing task is to make each arrow as short and as forced as possible. Many
